title: Taking without emptying: how much can we take and still leave enough?

summary.text: Fish, grass, clams and tigers all have babies every year, so they should never run out. Yet people have emptied lakes, seas and forests that refilled themselves for thousands of years. Your child counts beans they cannot see all at once, using the same trick scientists use for tigers and fish. They run a pond where a whole village shares the fish, and they see how a small mistake can empty it. They also build a model of groundwater, test which seeds in the kitchen are still alive, and find out why a village of rice farmers keeps five kinds of rice.
summary.art: A kitchen table with a glass jar of beans, a bowl of fish-shaped tokens beside a drawn pond, and a row of small paper seed packets.

intro.hook: Fill a jar with beans. Take out 40, mark each with a dot, and shake them back in. Now scoop out 40 beans again. Only 6 have a dot. Without counting the jar, how many beans are in it?
intro.text: You can work it out. If 6 of the 40 beans in the second scoop have a dot, then about 6 in every 40 beans in the jar have a dot. You marked 40 in all, so the jar holds about 40 times 40 divided by 6, which is about 270. Scientists use this trick to count fish in a lake and tigers in a forest, where nobody can count every one. In this unit you use it, and then you find out the harder question behind it. If fish, grass and trees all grow back, why do they still run out?
intro.art: A glass jar of dried chickpeas with a few beans marked with a dot, and a hand holding a cup of beans, three of them dotted.

outcomes: I can explain why something that regrows, such as fish, trees or clams, can still run out if we take it faster than it renews.
I can say what renewable and non-renewable mean, and give an example of each from my own home.
I can estimate how many there are of something I cannot count all at once, using mark and recapture, and say how I could make my estimate better.
I can explain why a group of animals that falls too low may not recover, even when we stop taking from it.
I can describe three ways people protect living things in India: protected places, village rules and saved seeds.
I can explain groundwater as a bank account, with water going in and water going out, using my own model.
I can give both sides of a hard question, such as bringing back an animal that has disappeared, and say what evidence I would want.

terms.meaning: Something nature makes again within a few years or a lifetime, such as fish, wood, grass and rainwater.
terms.example: Coconut palms in Kerala give nuts every month, year after year.
terms.art: A coconut palm with nuts, and a young palm growing beside her.

terms.meaning: Something nature makes so slowly that, for people, it is used up once it is gone, such as coal, oil and metal ores.
terms.example: Coal takes millions of years to form, so a lump burned today cannot be replaced.
terms.art: A lump of coal on a table next to a calendar showing millions of years.

terms.meaning: Used in a way that can go on for a very long time, because we take no more than nature renews.
terms.example: A village that catches only as many fish as are born each year can fish for ever.
terms.art: A fishing boat on a calm lake with a full net and many fish still swimming below.

terms.meaning: All the living beings of one kind in one place, such as all the rohu fish in a pond.
terms.example: The tigers living in one forest are a population.
terms.art: A group of spotted deer standing in a forest clearing.

terms.meaning: How many of something there are right now, such as the fish in a pond or the water under the ground.
terms.example: If a pond holds 24 fish today, the stock is 24.
terms.art: A pond drawn from the side with 24 small fish inside it.

terms.meaning: Catching fish faster than the fish can have young, so fewer and fewer are left.
terms.example: Off the coast of Newfoundland in Canada, too many cod were caught, and in 1992 fishing for them had to be stopped.
terms.art: A big net being pulled up, nearly empty, with only a few small fish.

terms.meaning: A small part of something that we look at closely, to learn about the whole.
terms.example: A cup of beans from a jar is a sample of the jar.
terms.art: A hand scooping a small cup of beans out of a big jar.

terms.meaning: A way to estimate how many there are. We mark some, let them go, catch some again, and see what fraction are marked.
terms.example: If 1 in 5 of the second catch is marked, then the marked ones are about 1 in 5 of the whole group.
terms.art: Fish being tagged with a tiny tag, then a second net holding some tagged and some untagged fish.

terms.meaning: A camera tied to a tree that takes a photo when an animal walks past. Scientists use it to count animals without disturbing them.
terms.example: Each tiger has different stripes, so camera trap photos show how many different tigers walk through a forest.
terms.art: A small camera strapped to a tree trunk and a tiger walking past in the dusk.

terms.meaning: No living member of that kind of animal or plant is left anywhere in the world.
terms.example: The dodo, a bird of the island of Mauritius, is extinct.
terms.art: A museum drawing of a dodo with a label that says gone for ever.

terms.meaning: In great danger of becoming extinct, because very few are left or their numbers are falling fast.
terms.example: The great Indian bustard, a big bird of dry grasslands, is endangered.
terms.art: A tall bird walking across dry grassland, with a small red warning sign beside her.

terms.meaning: The place where a living being finds her food, water, shelter and mates.
terms.example: A mangrove swamp is the habitat of fishing cats and many crabs.
terms.art: A mangrove forest with roots in the water, a crab on a root and a heron above.

terms.meaning: Breaking one big habitat into small separate pieces, for example with a road, a railway line or a farm.
terms.example: A highway across a forest can cut a tiger's walking range into two.
terms.art: A green forest cut in two by a wide road, with a deer stopped at the edge.

terms.meaning: A strip of land that joins two pieces of habitat, so animals can walk safely between them.
terms.example: An elephant underpass lets elephants walk beneath a road.
terms.art: A herd of elephants walking through a tunnel under a highway with cars passing above.

terms.meaning: A place the law or the community keeps for nature, such as a national park, a sanctuary or a sacred grove.
terms.example: Mudumalai in Tamil Nadu is a tiger reserve.
terms.art: A forest gate with a board that says national park, and a deer behind it.

terms.meaning: The many different kinds of living beings in a place, and the differences inside each kind.
terms.example: A forest with 200 kinds of trees has more biodiversity than a field of one crop.
terms.art: A crowded forest scene with many different plants, insects, birds and mammals.

terms.meaning: One kind of a crop, with its own taste, colour, size and way of facing weather and disease.
terms.example: Njavara, Gobindobhog and Chak-hao are three different varieties of rice.
terms.art: Three small bowls of rice grains, one red, one white and one black.

terms.meaning: A place that stores seeds safely, dry and cold, so a crop can be grown again if it is lost from the fields.
terms.example: India keeps seeds in a national gene bank in New Delhi.
terms.art: Shelves of labelled glass jars of seeds inside a cool room.

terms.meaning: An underground layer of sand, gravel or rock whose tiny spaces are full of water.
terms.example: A borewell pumps water out of an aquifer.
terms.art: A cut-away of the ground showing a layer of sand and gravel full of water, with a borewell reaching it.

terms.meaning: The top of the underground water. It goes up when rain soaks in and down when we pump more than refills.
terms.example: When many borewells are dug close together, the water table can fall by several metres in a few years.
terms.art: A cut-away of the ground with a blue dashed line showing the water table and a well reaching down to it.

terms.meaning: Water soaking down from the surface to refill the aquifer.
terms.example: A pit filled with stones lets terrace rain soak down and recharge a borewell.
terms.art: Rain falling from a terrace pipe into a pit of stones and sand, with arrows going down to the water below.

terms.meaning: Something a whole community shares and nobody owns alone, such as a village pond, a pasture, or a sea fishery.
terms.example: A village grazing ground that every family uses is a commons.
terms.art: A village pond with women filling pots, cows drinking and children playing at the edge.

terms.meaning: The amount we start from, when we measure whether something has grown or shrunk.
terms.example: If you remember a pond full of fish as a child, that is your baseline for how many fish a pond should have.
terms.art: A ruler with a mark at zero and a growing line of fish beside it.

explanations.concept: Renewable and non-renewable: what comes back, and how fast
explanations.definition: A renewable resource is one that nature makes again within a few years or a lifetime. A non-renewable resource takes so long to form that, for people, it is gone for ever once used.
explanations.description: Fish, grass, trees, rainwater and sunlight are renewable. Coal, petrol and metals are non-renewable, because they took millions of years to form. But renewable does not mean unlimited. A renewable thing comes back only at its own speed. A coconut palm gives nuts every month. A teak tree needs decades before she can be cut. Good soil forms so slowly that, for farmers, it behaves like a non-renewable thing. Groundwater deep under the ground can take hundreds of years to fill again. So the first question to ask about anything we take is not 'does it grow back?' but 'how fast does it grow back, and how fast are we taking it?'
examples: A fishing village takes fish, which have young every year. The fish are renewable, but only if enough are left to breed.
Coal in Jharkhand took millions of years to form. If we burn it, no new coal will form in our lifetime.
A borewell in a dry district may pump water that fell as rain a thousand years ago, so for us that water is almost non-renewable.
explanations.art: A timeline with a coconut palm at one year, a teak tree at forty years, and a lump of coal at millions of years.

explanations.concept: Stocks and flows: a pond as a bath with a tap and a drain
explanations.definition: A stock is how much of something there is right now. A flow is how fast it comes in or goes out. A stock stays steady when what comes in equals what goes out.
explanations.description: Think of a bath. The water in the bath is the stock. The tap is the flow coming in, and the drain is the flow going out. If the tap and the drain run at the same speed, the water level stays the same. If the drain runs faster, the bath slowly empties. A pond of fish works the same way. The fish in the pond are the stock. New fish being born is the tap. Fish caught, eaten by birds or lost to disease are the drain. The village controls only one drain, which is the catch. To keep a pond full, the catch must not be bigger than the births. In nature, the tap is not a fixed speed. It depends on how many parents there are, and that is what makes the story hard.
examples: A rooftop water tank has rain going in, taps taking water out, and the water level is the stock.
A forest has seedlings growing in, and trees cut or burned going out. If more are cut than grow, the forest shrinks.
A bank account has money coming in and going out. The balance is the stock.
explanations.art: A bathtub with a running tap labelled births and a drain labelled catch, drawn next to a pond with fish swimming.

explanations.concept: Parents matter: why a group that gets too small may not recover
explanations.definition: A group of animals makes its young from the animals that are left. If too few adults are left, too few young are born, and the group can keep shrinking even after people stop taking from it.
explanations.description: Imagine taking nearly all the fish from a pond. The few that are left may be too far apart to find each other, or too few to lay enough eggs. Each year there are fewer young, and the pond does not refill. Scientists say a group has fallen below a safe size. Off the coast of Newfoundland in Canada, huge numbers of cod were caught for hundreds of years. In 1992 the government stopped the cod fishery, because there were too few fish left. Many years later, the cod there had still not returned to their old numbers. Some groups come back quickly when we stop taking from them. Others do not. We cannot always tell in advance which is which.
examples: In the pond game, a pond with only 3 fish left cannot refill, because there are too few parents.
Tigers need large areas of forest and enough prey, so a tiger group that is small and split into pieces finds it hard to grow.
Vultures lay only one egg a year, so when most of them died, their numbers could not bounce back quickly.
explanations.art: Two ponds side by side: one with many fish and eggs, one with just two small fish far apart and no eggs.

explanations.concept: The sweet spot: the most we can take every year for ever
explanations.description: Some fisheries scientists use an idea called maximum sustainable yield. It is the biggest catch that can be taken every year for ever without the stock shrinking. In the pond game you will find it. If the pond is nearly empty, there are few parents, so few young are born. If the pond is full, the fish crowd each other and fewer grow. The most new fish appear when the pond is somewhere in the middle. If you catch only that many new fish each year, the pond stays the same. This is a simple picture. Real lakes and seas change with the weather, the food and the other animals, so the sweet spot moves from year to year. Many scientists now say it is safer to catch somewhat less than the largest amount, to leave room for mistakes.
examples: In the pond game, leaving 16 fish each year and catching the rest gives the biggest steady catch.
A fishing community may agree to catch less than the maximum, in case a bad monsoon year comes.
Grass is cut or grazed more often in wet years than in dry years, because the sweet spot is higher when there is more rain.
explanations.art: A hill-shaped graph where the horizontal line is the number of fish left in the pond and the vertical line is the number of new fish born, peaking in the middle.

explanations.concept: Counting what you cannot see: samples, marking and camera traps
explanations.definition: When we cannot count every one, we count a sample and work out the rest. In mark and recapture, we mark some, release them, catch a second sample, and use the fraction that are marked to estimate the whole group.
explanations.description: Suppose you mark 40 fish and let them go. Later you catch 40 fish, and 8 of them have a mark. So 8 out of 40, or 1 in 5, of the fish are marked. The 40 you marked are one fifth of the whole lake. So the lake holds about 5 times 40, which is 200 fish. As a rule, the group size is about the first marked number times the second catch, divided by the marked ones in the second catch. This works only if the marked ones mix in with the others, and if they do not die or leave. For tigers, scientists do not need to mark them. Every tiger has a different pattern of stripes, so a camera trap photo is like a fingerprint. India's tiger counts now use thousands of camera traps. Older counts used footprints, which were harder to tell apart. A sample is always a little different from the truth, so careful scientists count many times and give a range.
examples: Scientists tag a few hundred turtles on a beach and later see how many tagged turtles come back, to estimate how many turtles use that beach.
Camera traps in a forest in Karnataka photograph a tiger from both sides, and her stripes are matched against earlier photos.
The Asian Waterbird Census asks volunteers to count birds at wetlands every January, and the counts from many years are compared.
explanations.art: A lake with fish, some with red tags, and a net holding eight tagged and thirty-two untagged fish, with a calculation written beside it.

explanations.concept: The shifting baseline: when every generation thinks their nature is normal
explanations.definition: The shifting baseline is a habit of mind. Each generation takes the amount of nature they first met as normal, so a slow loss over many generations goes unnoticed.
explanations.description: In 1995 a fisheries scientist named Daniel Pauly described this habit. A grandmother may remember a lake full of big fish. Her granddaughter grows up seeing fewer and smaller fish, and thinks that is how a lake always is. When her own granddaughter is born, the lake may be almost empty, and the child thinks that is normal too. No single year felt like a disaster, but together they were. This is why scientists do not trust memory alone. They look for old records, such as fishing logs, old photographs, museum shells and bones, and the sizes of fish landed in markets. When a village notices that the biggest fish in the market are smaller every decade, that is a clue, even if the catch in baskets looks the same.
examples: The size of the biggest clam or fish in the market each year is a record. If it falls over many years, the group is probably being caught too young.
An elder in Kerala remembers many sparrows on the roof, and a child today may think a few is normal.
Old photographs of a lake or a beach, taken from the same place over the years, can show changes that people forgot.
explanations.art: Three generations standing by the same lake, with big fish in the first picture, small fish in the second, and almost none in the third.

explanations.concept: Places kept for nature: parks, reserves, sacred groves and village rules
explanations.definition: A protected area is a place where the law or the community limits what people may take, so that living beings can keep their homes.
explanations.description: India passed the Wildlife (Protection) Act in 1972, and began Project Tiger in 1973 to save tigers. Today India has more than a hundred national parks, and many sanctuaries and tiger reserves. Counts reported by the government show about 1,400 tigers in 2006 and more than 3,000 in 2022. Protected places are not only made by governments. Villages have kept sacred groves for hundreds of years. In Meghalaya, the Mawphlang sacred forest is kept by local people, and no one may cut a branch. In Rajasthan, village pastures called orans are kept for grazing and trees. In Kerala, small forest patches called kavu are kept near temples. Scientists find that many of these small, old groves hold plants and animals that have disappeared from the land around them.
examples: Mudumalai Tiger Reserve in Tamil Nadu, joined to forests in Karnataka and Kerala, lets tigers and elephants walk between forests.
Sacred groves in Karnataka, known as devarakadu, hold old trees and small streams.
A fishing village on the east coast may agree not to fish near a beach where olive ridley turtles nest in winter.
explanations.art: A map of south India with small green marks for tiger reserves, sacred groves and a turtle nesting beach.

explanations.concept: Room to move: why a cut-up forest holds fewer kinds of life
explanations.definition: Habitat fragmentation is breaking a large habitat into small separate pieces. A wildlife corridor is a strip of habitat that joins the pieces again.
explanations.description: A big forest holds more kinds of living beings than a small patch. Large animals such as elephants and tigers walk long distances for food and water, and to find mates. When a road, a railway or a farm cuts the forest in two, the animals on each side are trapped in a smaller space. Small groups have fewer parents, and the animals may become too closely related. The animals also die crossing roads and railway lines. To help, people build corridors of forest and tunnels under roads. A study in India found that tigers do use highway underpasses built for them. Scientists agree that bigger and better-joined habitats hold more kinds of life, but they still argue about the best size and shape of reserves.
examples: Elephants in the Western Ghats follow routes used for hundreds of years, and the corridors that join forest patches keep those routes open.
Some highways in India have underpasses for tigers and other animals, and cameras record who uses them.
A garden with a hedge and a few trees can be a small corridor for butterflies and birds across a city.
explanations.art: A forest cut by a road, with a green tunnel under the road and an elephant walking through it.

explanations.concept: A seed is a saved story: why many varieties matter
explanations.definition: A crop variety is one kind of a crop with its own taste, colour and strengths. Keeping many varieties alive, in fields and in seed banks, protects a crop from failing all at once.
explanations.description: In the 1840s, the farmers of Ireland grew mostly one kind of potato. A disease called blight spread, the potatoes rotted in the ground, and about a million people died of hunger. When every field has the same variety, one disease can take all of them. Indian farmers have grown tens of thousands of varieties of rice, millets, pulses and vegetables, each shaped by its own place. Some stand floods, some stand drought, some taste better and some keep longer. Scientists use these old varieties to breed new ones. A flood-tolerant rice from Odisha called FR13A was used to breed a modern rice that can survive under flood water for about two weeks. Seed banks keep seeds dry and cold. India's national gene bank is in New Delhi, and the Svalbard vault in Norway, opened in 2008, keeps copies from many countries. M. S. Swaminathan, the Indian scientist who helped bring high-yielding wheat and rice to India, also spent many years urging that old varieties be kept safe.
examples: A farmer in Kerala keeps a little Njavara rice for her family, and several other kinds for the market.
Millets such as ragi, kodo and foxtail millet stand drought better than many crops, so some farmers are growing them again.
A seed library lets neighbours borrow seed, grow it, and return some seed from the harvest.
explanations.art: Five small baskets of rice of different colours, with a blight cloud over one basket.

explanations.definition: Groundwater is water held in an aquifer under the ground. Rain soaking in is a deposit, and pumping out is a withdrawal. If we take out more than goes in, the water table falls.
explanations.description: Imagine a bank account. Rain soaking into the ground is money coming in. Borewells and wells are money going out. If you take out more than you put in, the balance falls, and one day it is zero. In many parts of India, thousands of borewells pump from the same aquifer, and the water table has fallen by many metres. Digging deeper is like taking a loan from your future. Roads and roofs make it worse, because rain runs off them into drains instead of soaking in. Near the coast there is another danger. When the fresh water falls, salt water from the sea can slowly seep into the aquifer, and wells turn salty. This has been reported in some areas near Chennai. People refill the account with rainwater harvesting, with ponds and tanks, and with johads, which are small earth dams that hold monsoon rain on the land. In Alwar in Rajasthan, villagers and a group called Tarun Bharat Sangh built thousands of johads, and wells and a small river that had dried up were reported to flow again.
examples: In your tub model, the water level drops near the well you pump, and a well close to it also dries up.
A temple tank in Madurai or Kanchipuram soaks water into the ground and helps the wells around it.
A pit of stones and sand under a downpipe sends rain from a terrace down to the aquifer.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the ground with an aquifer, a rain arrow going in, a borewell pumping out, and a measuring stick showing the water table falling.

explanations.concept: Do shared things always get used up? The tragedy of the commons
explanations.description: A commons is a resource that a whole community shares, such as a village pond, a pasture or a sea fishery. In 1968 an American scientist named Garrett Hardin wrote an essay with the title The Tragedy of the Commons. He pictured a pasture that every herder shares. Each herder gains by adding one more cow, but the cost of too much grazing is shared by everyone. So every herder adds a cow, and the pasture is ruined. The pond game lets you feel this pull. But is it always true? Elinor Ostrom, an American scientist, studied many real commons, from mountain meadows in Switzerland to irrigation systems in Spain and fisheries in Turkey. She found many communities that had looked after a commons for hundreds of years, using their own rules. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics for this work. People still argue about which rules work best, and when.
examples: Many open seas have been overfished, because no single country or village controls them.
The oran grazing lands of Rajasthan and many village ponds have been managed by communities for generations.
A class that shares one set of crayons can finish them very fast, or share them well, depending on the rules.
explanations.art: A village pasture with cows and herders around a small circle of stones, and a group of women and men talking at the centre.

perspectives.explanation: When many people share something and nobody owns it, each person gains by taking more, and the cost falls on everyone. So shared things are used up unless someone sets strict rules or divides the resource into private parts.

Real communities often solve this problem themselves. They know who may use the commons, set limits, watch each other, punish cheating fairly and talk often. Their rules work best when the people who use the commons help to make the rules.

Both can be true. Small groups who know each other manage well. Large open seas, with many boats from many places and no shared rules, are the hardest to protect, and they need agreements between countries.

explanations.concept: Should we bring back animals that have disappeared? The cheetah in India
explanations.description: Asiatic cheetahs once ran across India's grasslands. They were declared extinct in India in 1952. In September 2022, eight cheetahs from Namibia in Africa were brought by aeroplane to Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh, and more came from South Africa in 2023. The plan is to start a group of cheetahs in India and help the dry grasslands that they live in. Some of the cheetahs have died since, and scientists and officials have argued about whether the plan is wise. This is called reintroduction, and it is being tried in many countries. The cheetahs are of an African kind, not the Asiatic cheetah that once lived here, and that is part of the argument. No one yet knows how it will end.
examples: Gray wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park in the United States in 1995, and some scientists report that the rivers and trees changed as the deer moved.
The one-horned rhino in Assam recovered from very few animals a century ago, after strong protection.
Gharials, a long-snouted crocodile of Indian rivers, are bred in centres and released into rivers like the Chambal.
explanations.art: A cheetah standing in tall grassland near a forest guard's jeep, with a long fence in the distance.

perspectives.explanation: India lost its cheetahs. Grasslands, which are shrinking, also need protecting. A new group of cheetahs brings money and attention to grassland animals that are also in danger, such as the great Indian bustard.

The African cheetahs are a different kind from the Asiatic cheetah that lived here. The money and land might be better spent on animals that are still alive in India, and the cheetahs need a lot of space to live.

perspectives.who: Scientists who want to wait and see
perspectives.explanation: Reintroduction sometimes works and sometimes fails. The honest answer is to keep careful records for many years, and to share what is learned, before saying whether it was worth it.

agreed.text: A group of living beings stays about the same size when the new ones born equal the ones lost. It grows when more are born than lost, and shrinks when fewer are born.
agreed.evidence: Counts of fish, birds and trees over many years across the world follow this pattern. You can see it in the pond game.

agreed.text: A group that is caught faster than it can replace itself will shrink, and a group that falls very low may not recover even when people stop.
agreed.evidence: The cod of Newfoundland were stopped in 1992 and had still not fully returned many years later. Vulture numbers in India fell by more than nine in every ten and have recovered only slowly.

agreed.text: A careful sample can tell us nearly the true size of a group we cannot count, if the sample is big, taken in a fair way, and the marked ones mix with the rest.
agreed.evidence: Scientists check mark and recapture by using it on groups they can count in the end, such as beans in a jar. Estimates get closer to the truth when the samples get bigger.

agreed.text: Big, joined-up habitats hold more kinds of life than small, cut-up ones.
agreed.evidence: Surveys of forest patches of different sizes in many countries find that bigger patches hold more kinds of plants and animals.

agreed.text: Groundwater falls when more is pumped out than soaks in.
agreed.evidence: Government and university teams measure water levels in thousands of wells in India, and compare them year after year. In many districts the levels fall in the dry months and when pumping increases.

agreed.text: A farm or a village that grows many varieties of a crop is less likely to lose everything to one disease or one bad season.
agreed.evidence: The potato famine in Ireland in the 1840s followed a single variety. Field trials in China, where rice farmers planted two varieties in the same field, found that disease was much lower than in fields with one variety.

challenging.claim: If something grows back, we can take as much of it as we like.
challenging.who: Many people, and many old fishing and farming practices.
challenging.for: Fish, grass and trees do have young. Some groups recover quickly after heavy catches.
challenging.against: Regrowth needs parents. If we take too many, there are too few parents left. The cod of Newfoundland were renewable, and yet they were caught down to a point from which they did not quickly recover.

challenging.claim: If the catch in the baskets is the same every day, the lake must be healthy.
challenging.who: Many fishers and market traders, in many places.
challenging.for: A full basket feels like a full lake, and it can stay full for years if the fishers go further or use finer nets.
challenging.against: The baskets may hold more, smaller fish each year. Scientists look at the size of the fish, and at how long it takes to catch a basket. Shrinking size is an early warning.

challenging.claim: Once we stop catching, a fish stock will quickly bounce back.
challenging.who: A hopeful idea held by many people.
challenging.for: Some stocks have recovered in a few years after a ban, such as certain herring in the North Sea.
challenging.against: Other stocks, such as the cod of Newfoundland, took decades and had not fully returned. A group that has fallen very low may have lost its old breeding places and its range of kinds.

challenging.claim: Only experts and governments can look after nature.
challenging.who: A view held by many officials in the twentieth century.
challenging.for: Governments can pass laws, pay guards and run research. Some common resources are too big for one village.
challenging.against: Village councils called Van Panchayats have managed forests in Uttarakhand for nearly a hundred years. Sacred groves, orans and village ponds were protected for centuries by communities. Elinor Ostrom's studies found many communities that managed commons well.

challenging.claim: Saving one famous animal is enough. The rest will be fine.
challenging.for: A famous animal like a tiger or a rhino can bring money and attention. Protecting her forest also protects many others.
challenging.against: An animal needs her food, her water and her place to live. When vultures were poisoned by a painkiller, nobody had been hunting vultures, yet most of them died. Protecting only the animal, and not what she depends on, may not be enough.

challenging.claim: Old crop varieties are old-fashioned. Only new high-yield varieties matter.
challenging.for: High-yielding wheat and rice, introduced in the 1960s, helped India grow far more food and avoid famine.
challenging.against: Old varieties carry useful traits, such as standing floods or drought. A rice variety from Odisha was used to breed a flood-tolerant rice. Losing old varieties means losing the raw material for new ones.

big_questions.q: A pond holds 24 fish, and the village catches 8 every year, and the pond is full again each spring. If they catch 9 each year instead, what do you think happens in the long run? Why?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many parents are left each time, and whether one extra fish a year could ever be noticed.

big_questions.q: In mark and recapture, we assume the marked beans mix evenly with the others. What would go wrong if the marked beans sank to the bottom of the jar?
big_questions.hint: Think about which beans your second scoop would pick up.

big_questions.q: A fisherwoman brings home a full basket of clams each day, just like her grandmother did. But her clams are half the size. Is the lake healthy?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a basket measures, and what size tells you about age.

big_questions.q: Who does a fish in the open sea belong to? Who does the water under your street belong to?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is allowed to take it, who is allowed to stop them, and who is not there to speak.

big_questions.q: Tigers do not know where a reserve's boundary is. Should the edge of a park be drawn where the tiger lives, or where people agree to draw a line?
big_questions.hint: Think about the animal, the villagers who live at the edge, and the farmers whose crops she may eat.

big_questions.q: A village has five kinds of rice. In a good year, the best kind gives the most grain. Why might the village still keep all five?
big_questions.hint: Think about a year when one disease or one flood comes.

big_questions.q: Your grandparents say there were many more birds when they were children. How could you find out if they are right?
big_questions.hint: Think about old photographs, bird records, or counting a place the same way each year.

big_questions.q: Is there a right number of tigers, or of fish in a lake? Is that number a fact in nature, or something people agree on?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a tiger needs, what the villagers need, and who gets to decide.

big_questions.q: When we protect a forest for tigers, we also protect water, insects, trees and many other animals. Is the tiger the reason, or one of many reasons?
big_questions.hint: Think about who benefits and who is left out when only one famous animal is the reason.

story.title: The Shelf of Shells
story.note: A made-up story. Meenu, Ammamma, Saji and their village are invented. True: Ashtamudi Lake near Kollam in Kerala is a large backwater where clams are collected, mostly by women, by wading and diving. The fishery there is reported to follow rules on size and season, and was reported to have been certified as sustainable in 2014. Meenu's shells, with sizes of 7 centimetres falling to 3, are invented to show an idea that fisheries scientists really use: the size of what is caught, measured year after year.
text: Meenu lived in a small house beside Ashtamudi Lake, near Kollam in Kerala. The lake was wide and green-brown, with coconut palms leaning over the water. Every morning, before school, she heard the thump of her grandmother's boat against the steps.

Her grandmother was Ammamma, and Ammamma was a clam collector. For forty years she had waded and dived in the shallow lake before sunrise. She felt for clams with her toes and her fingers, and dropped them into a basket tied at her waist.

On the shelf above the kitchen window sat a row of clam shells. Under each one, in white chalk, was a number. Thirty-one shells, from 1 to 31. "Each year I keep the biggest clam I find," Ammamma said. "Don't touch."

In the school holidays, Meenu was finally allowed to go out in the boat. Ammamma gave her a steel ring as wide as a bangle. "Any clam that slips through this ring is too small," she said. "They go back in the water."

Meenu found a clam, then another. Half of them slipped through the ring. She put them back, one by one, and the basket filled slowly. "Ammamma, it would be much faster if we kept the small ones too," she said.
"Faster today," said Ammamma. "Slower every year after."

A boat came close. It was Saji, their neighbour, with a rake that had very fine teeth. He dragged it along the bottom and tipped a pile of clams of every size into his boat. "Why leave the little ones?" he called. "If you don't take them, someone else will."
Ammamma did not answer. She only pulled up her basket and rowed home.

That evening, Meenu could not stop thinking. She had a science lesson at school. Her teacher, Jaya Miss, had taught the class that you can learn about a big thing by measuring a small part of it, and that it is better to measure the same way every time. Meenu looked up at the shelf of shells.

She took down her school bag, found her ruler, and carefully took down the first shell. It was as wide as her palm. She measured it, and wrote 7 centimetres in her notebook. Then she took the tenth shell. It was 6 centimetres. The twentieth was 5. The last one, from this year, was 3.
She stood the shells in a line on the table, from the oldest to the newest. The line ran downhill, like a staircase going down. She drew it on paper, and it made the same shape.

Ammamma came in from the kitchen and stopped. "I have looked at those shells every day," she said slowly. "Every year, the new one looked about right. I never lined them up." She touched the first shell. "When I was young, one clam like this filled my hand."
The next Thursday there was a meeting in the village hall. The men said the baskets were full, just as always. "The lake is as rich as ever," Saji said. "Why are we talking about rings and rules?"
Meenu stood up. Her knees shook. She put her thirty-one shells on the table in order, and she held up her paper. "The baskets are full," she said. "But look at what is in them."
The hall went quiet. A woman at the back said, "My basket is full of babies." Another said, "My mother told me the clams were as big as her fist."
Saji picked up the first shell and then the last. He turned them over in his hands for a long time. "Is this what we have been doing?" he said at last. "Eating the children?"

They made a plan that night. Everyone would use a ring, the same size for all. For one month, when the clams release their young into the water, nobody would collect at all. And every year, each collector would keep the biggest clam they found, and Meenu would measure them in a row.

A year later, the new shell on Ammamma's shelf was 4 centimetres across. It was not much. But it was the first shell in thirty-two years that was bigger than the one before. Ammamma wrote the number 32 under it in white chalk, and then she wrote 4 beside it.
story.epiphany: A full basket tells you how much was caught, not how much is left. The size of what we catch, measured the same way every year, shows whether the young are getting time to grow.
ask: Why can a fisher's basket stay full while a lake slowly runs out of clams?
What could a village measure every year to find out whether its lake is being fished too hard?
Why does a rule that sends small clams back help even the people who follow it, if some neighbours do not follow it?
Why did it matter that Meenu measured the shells the same way every time?

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1990s, bird watchers in India noticed something strange. Vultures, once so common that they circled over every village, were becoming rare. Many scientists thought an infection was killing them. A scientist at the Bombay Natural History Society, Vibhu Prakash, and his team counted the vultures again and again, along the same roads and in the same places each year. Their counts showed that in some places, more than nine in every ten birds were gone. The cause was still a puzzle. In 2004, a team led by the scientist Lindsay Oaks tested dead vultures in Pakistan and found that their kidneys had failed. The cause was a painkiller for cattle called diclofenac. When a farmer treated a sick cow or buffalo with it and the animal died, the vultures that fed on her body were poisoned. India banned the cattle medicine in 2006. The wrong idea was that an infection was killing the birds. A careful look at the dead birds found poison in the food chain.
how_we_found_out.who: Vibhu Prakash and the Bombay Natural History Society, with Lindsay Oaks and a team that included scientists in Pakistan
how_we_found_out.when: Counts from the 1990s, the cause found in 2004, and the ban on the cattle medicine in 2006
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought an infectious disease was killing India's vultures. Careful counts showed how fast they were disappearing, and tests on dead birds showed that a cattle painkiller was poisoning them.

roots.context: We have counted beans, run a pond and built a model of groundwater. Now we ask what counting and taking tell us about how we know the living world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: No one can see a whole group of fish or tigers at once. We count a sample and work out the rest. Each generation also takes the nature they grew up with as normal. So 'how much is left' has to be measured, because memory moves.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'how much nature is left' is something we can simply look at, like eggs in a tray. We trust what our eyes see now, and what we remember as normal.
deep_truth.evidence: In the bean jar, nobody saw all the beans, yet a few scoops gave a good estimate. In the Ask an Elder activity, the list of what used to be here changed with the age of the person. If your results differ, write them as they are and say why.

three.who_am_i: Your eyes and ears take a small sample of the world, and your mind works out the rest. A bee takes a different sample, and a bat takes another.
three.what_is_life: A group of fish goes on for thousands of years, though each fish lives only a few. Births and deaths flow through the group like water through a pond.
three.what_is_this_world: Fish in a lake, water under the ground and seeds in a jar are all stocks with a tap and a drain. Most of these flows are slower and bigger than one human life.

roots.thread: One fish is one life. A pond of fish is a group that goes on across many lives, held together by the births and deaths that flow through it. The fisher, the heron and the otter each take a few, and the pond lasts as long as the flows balance. Nobody stands outside the pond. A fisher is one of the beings taking from it, and one of the beings it feeds.

teachings.teaching: The Earth is my mother, and I am her child.
teachings.link: A child is born of the pond and belongs to it, and cannot count the fish from outside. Counting the stock carefully is one way to pay attention to the mother who feeds us.

teachings.teaching: Knowing what is enough saves us from shame. Knowing when to stop saves us from danger, and so we can last a long time.
teachings.link: In the pond game, the biggest steady catch comes from stopping at the right point. A village that knows when to stop can fish for ever.

teachings.teaching: As a bee takes nectar from a flower and flies away without harming her colour or scent, so should a wise person move through a village.
teachings.link: A bee takes from the flower and helps the flower make seeds. Taking in a way that leaves the source whole is what the ring on Ammamma's boat does.

science.text: Mark and recapture and camera traps let scientists estimate groups that no one can count, and a careful estimate always comes with a range.
About two million kinds of living beings have been named, but nobody knows how many there are in all. Estimates run from several million to many millions.

other_view.who: Many elders and keepers of traditional knowledge
other_view.view: Memory is not always unreliable. When a community keeps its memory in stories, songs and calendars, and checks it together, it can notice a slow change long before a scientist measures it. The shifting baseline is a danger mainly when memory is kept by one person alone.

practice.title: Count a handful, guess the rest
practice.say: Sit with a bowl of beans. Take a handful and set them in a second bowl, one bean for each slow breath. Count them. Now say how many you think are left in the first bowl, without counting. Notice how much you know and how much you are guessing. Close your eyes and think of a lake you cannot see all at once.
practice.kid: Take a handful of beans. Put them in a bowl, one for each breath. Count them. Guess how many are left. Notice what you know and what you guess.

ask: When you say there used to be more birds, how do you know? Is it your memory, a record, or both?
If we can never count everything, how sure should we be of an estimate before we act on it?
Who in your family remembers a place differently from you? What might each of you be leaving out?
roots.art: A girl holding up one scoop of beans with a large jar behind her, and a faint picture of a whole lake in the clouds above.

games.title: Pond Council: how many fish can the village take?
games.context: This is a game about a village that shares one pond of fish for eight years. Each year every villager chooses how many fish to catch. You find out how many fish a pond can give for ever.

setup.art: A drawn pond with 16 dried beans as fish inside it, an empty bowl in front of each of three players, and a year track with eight boxes.
setup.caption: 1. Put 16 fish in the pond. Give each villager a bowl.

setup.art: Three fists held out over the table, each holding some beans, and a child writing the number 3 in a table.
setup.caption: 2. Each year, everyone holds out a fist with the fish they want to catch.

setup.art: A hand taking beans from the pond into bowls, then a child adding new beans, one for every two left.
setup.caption: 3. Take the catch. Count what is left. Add 1 new fish for every 2 left.

setup.art: A pond with 3 beans left and a red cross over it, and a note that reads: too few parents.
setup.caption: 4. If 3 or fewer fish are left, the pond is lost and everyone loses.

printables.title: Pond board: a pond with 24 fish spaces, and a track of 8 years
items: The pond: draw a big oval and mark 24 small circles inside it, for the fish.
A table with a row for each year and three columns for the three villagers' catches.

printables.title: Fish tokens: 24 dried beans, buttons or paper fish
items: Fish token: a dried bean, a button or a small paper fish. You need 24.
Villager bowl: a small bowl or a circle on paper for each player to keep their catch.
Year marker: a coin or a bottle cap that moves along the year track.

printables.title: 12 weather cards, to use from the second game onwards
items: Good rains. Add 2 fish to the pond, up to 24.
Good rains. Add 2 fish to the pond, up to 24.
Good rains. Add 2 fish to the pond, up to 24.
Hot summer. Take 2 fish out of the pond, if there are 2 or more.
Hot summer. Take 2 fish out of the pond, if there are 2 or more.
Hot summer. Take 2 fish out of the pond, if there are 2 or more.

rules: Put 16 fish tokens in the pond. Each player is one villager, and gets a bowl. Put the year marker on Year 1.
Each year has three parts: the catch, the count and the breeding. From the second game, add a fourth part, the weather.

The catch: every player secretly holds 0 to 4 beans in a closed fist. These are the fish they want to catch. Everyone opens their fist together. Each player takes that many fish from the pond into their bowl. If the pond has fewer fish than were asked for, take turns taking one fish each until none are left.
The count: count the fish left in the pond. If 3 or fewer fish are left, the pond is lost. There are too few parents to have young. Everyone loses.
The breeding: if 4 or more fish are left, add 1 new fish for every 2 fish left. Ignore a leftover single fish. The pond holds at most 24 fish.
The weather: turn over a weather card and do what it says. Put the card at the bottom of the pile.
After 8 years, if the pond is still alive, the villager with the most fish in their bowl wins. If two have the same, they share the win.

The Council game: before each year, players may talk and agree on how many fish each will catch. The village wins together if the pond is alive after 8 years and all the bowls hold at least 40 fish in all.
Playing alone: play all three villagers yourself. Win by catching at least 45 fish in 8 years while the pond stays alive.

flow.context: This is the first step of Pond Council. You set up the pond, the bowls and the year track.
flow.do: Draw the pond board. Put 16 fish tokens in the pond. Give each player a bowl. Put the year marker on Year 1.
flow.say: This pond has 16 fish. We are three villagers, and we all live from this pond. Fish have young every year. Let's find out how many we can catch.
flow.kid: Draw a pond. Put 16 beans in it. Each player gets a bowl.
flow.parent: Three players works best. With two, one player plays two villagers. Keep the weather cards aside for now. Dried beans can choke a child under five, so keep them away from little ones. With four villagers, use the same 16 fish. It gets tighter, which is part of the lesson. With one child and a parent, the parent plays one villager and the child plays two.

flow.context: In this step you play one greedy year, to see what happens when every villager takes as much as they can.
flow.do: Play Year 1 with every villager catching 4 fish. Take 12 fish from the pond. Count what is left. Then add 1 new fish for every 2 left.
flow.say: Imagine we are all very hungry. Each of us catches 4 fish. That is 12 fish. How many are left in the pond? How many young fish will be born?
flow.kid: Everyone catches 4 fish. Take 12 out. Count what is left. Add new fish.

ask.q: Next year, if everyone catches 4 again, what will happen to the pond?
good: There are only 6 fish, so 12 cannot be caught.
The pond will be lost, because too few parents are left.
There will be almost no fish left.

check.q: After the catch, 10 fish are left in a pond. For every 2 fish, 1 new fish is born. How many fish are in the pond after breeding?
check.why: 10 fish make 5 pairs, so 5 new fish are born. 10 plus 5 is 15. Picking 20 means thinking every fish has one young, but only each pair does.

flow.parent: Greedy play leaves 4 fish, which breed to 6. The pond is not lost yet, but it is almost empty. Say nothing about what is right. Let the children see the numbers.

flow.context: In this step you start a new game and play Years 1 to 4, where each villager chooses their own catch in secret.
flow.do: Reset the pond to 16 fish. Play Years 1 to 4. Each year, everyone holds out a fist, takes the catch, counts and breeds. Write each catch in the table.
flow.say: Now we play for real. Think about your own bowl, and about the pond. How many fish will you try for this year?
flow.kid: Reset the pond to 16. Play four years. Write each catch in the table.

ask.q: How did you choose how many fish to catch?
good: I took a few and left more to breed.
I took the same as the others did.
I was worried the others would take them, so I took more.

flow.think: Did you ever want to catch more because you thought someone else would?
flow.parent: Notice who takes 0 in Year 1. A pond of 16 fish becomes 24 if nobody fishes, so waiting one year can give a bigger catch later.

flow.context: In this step you finish the game with Years 5 to 8 and find out who wins, or whether the pond was lost.
flow.do: Play Years 5 to 8. After Year 8, count the fish in each bowl. Add them up. Write down if the pond is alive.
flow.say: Years 5 to 8. Count the fish in the pond each year before you decide. Is the pond staying full, or getting smaller?
flow.kid: Play years 5 to 8. Count the bowls at the end.

ask.q: What happened in Year 8? Did anyone take extra fish at the end, and why?
good: Some took more because the game was ending.
No one took extra, because they wanted the pond to last.
It was hard to take less when it was the last year.

flow.parent: If the pond was lost, say so gently and ask what could be done. If it survived, ask what the pond looked like before each catch. The village's best total over 8 years is 64 fish, but only by leaving 16 fish each year.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pond Council. You play the Council version, where the villagers talk and agree a rule before each year.
flow.do: Reset the pond to 16 fish. Play 8 years again. Before each year, everyone talks and agrees how many each villager will catch. Count the fish at the end.
flow.say: This time we can talk first, like a village council. What rule will we agree, so that every villager is fed and the pond lasts?
flow.kid: Reset the pond. Talk first. Agree a rule. Then play.

check.q: A pond holds at most 24 fish. After the catch, 16 fish are left. How many fish will be in the pond after breeding?
check.why: 16 fish make 8 pairs, so 8 new fish are born. 16 plus 8 is 24, which is the most the pond can hold. So leaving 16 gives the biggest steady catch of 8 fish a year.

flow.think: How was the game different when you could talk? What did a rule do that a promise could not?

games.title: Seed Keepers: a village with five kinds of rice
games.context: This is a game about farm families who grow five kinds of rice in one village. Some years a disease wipes out one kind. You find out why it helps to grow many kinds and to save seed.

printables.title: Farm sheet, one for each family

One seed jar box. Blight cannot harm seed in a jar.

rules: Two to four players are farm families in one village. Each family draws a farm sheet with five field boxes, a seed jar box and a grain tally.

At the start, each family secretly writes one of the five varieties in each field box. They can write all five the same, or five different. They also write one variety in the seed jar. Then everyone reveals their sheet.
Each year, turn over the top trouble card. A blight card names one variety. Every field of that variety, in every family's sheet, fails. Rub it out. Seed in a jar is not harmed.
Harvest: each full field gives 1 grain. A Gobindobhog field gives 2 grains, because it sells for double.
Hungry year: if a family has fewer than 3 full fields after the trouble card, they must borrow grain. They give back 3 grains from their tally, but the tally cannot go below zero.

Replanting: each family may fill one empty field box with any variety that is in someone's field or someone's seed jar. A family may also change their seed jar to any variety they have in a full field.
A variety is extinct if it is in no field and in no seed jar. Cross it off the list for ever. Nobody can plant it again.
After 8 years, every extinct variety costs every family 3 grains. The family with the most grain left wins.
Playing alone: play two families yourself. Try to finish with all five varieties alive.

flow.context: This is the first step of Seed Keepers. You draw the farm sheets and choose your first crops.
flow.do: Each family draws a farm sheet. Lay out the five variety cards. Each family writes a variety in each of five boxes, and one in the seed jar. Do it in secret.
flow.say: You are a farm family. Choose what to grow in each of your five fields. You can grow one kind or many. Pick one kind to keep in your seed jar.
flow.kid: Draw five boxes and a jar. Write a rice in each. Keep it secret.
flow.parent: Do not explain the blight yet. Let the children choose without knowing what is coming. You need no special items: use scrap paper for the sheets and cut paper for the cards. Two to four players. Alone, play two families.

flow.context: In this step you reveal the farms and play the first year, to see what a blight does.
flow.do: Reveal the farm sheets. Turn over the first trouble card. Rub out the fields it names. Count the grain for each family. Write it in the tally.
flow.say: Look at everyone's farms. Now the first trouble card. Whose fields failed? Who had many kinds, and who had one?
flow.kid: Show your farm. Turn over a card. Rub out the failed fields. Count your grain.

check.q: A family grew only Gobindobhog in all five fields. Blight hits Gobindobhog. How many fields give grain this year?
check.why: A blight takes every field of the variety it names. A family with one variety loses everything at once. A family with five varieties would lose only one field.

flow.parent: With a lucky first card, nobody loses. Say that luck runs out. Keep playing.

flow.context: In this step you play Years 2 to 5. Families replant and decide which seed to save in their jar.
flow.do: Play Years 2 to 5. Each year: turn over a trouble card, rub out failed fields, harvest, then replant one empty box. Change your seed jar if you wish.
flow.say: Each year, ask yourself: which kind do I want to keep in my jar? Which kind might be lost? Who can give me seed?
flow.kid: Play four years. Replant one empty box each year. Keep a seed in your jar.

check.q: Blight hits Chak-hao. No family has Chak-hao in a seed jar. Can anyone plant it again?
check.why: In this game, a variety is extinct when it is in no field and no jar. Seed saved in a jar is the only way back. This is why people save seed from the harvest every year.

ask.q: Which variety are you glad someone kept in a jar?
good: The one that failed this year.
The one that nobody was growing.
The one that might do well in a flood or a dry year.

flow.context: In this step you play Years 6 to 8 and then count the grain, to find out which farm families did best.
flow.do: Play Years 6 to 8. After Year 8, check the list. Take 3 grains from every family for each extinct variety. Count who has the most grain.
flow.say: Last three years. Then we count the grain, and we count the varieties. Are all five still alive?
flow.kid: Play the last three years. Cross out extinct rice. Count your grain.

ask.q: Did growing one variety ever pay off, and did it ever cost you?
good: Gobindobhog gave double grain until the blight came.
When blight hit my one kind, I lost everything.
Having many kinds meant I lost only a few fields.

flow.parent: If a variety became extinct, let that be the main talking point. Ask who could have saved it.

flow.context: This is the last step of Seed Keepers. You talk about what the game showed you about real farms.
flow.do: Ask the questions below and let everyone answer.
flow.say: Real farmers once grew thousands of kinds of rice. Why would a village keep a rice that nobody is buying this year?
flow.kid: Why keep a rice nobody wants this year?
flow.think: Which rice might you be glad to have, if a flood or a drought comes?

experiments.title: Beans in the Jar: how many are there, if you cannot count them all at once?
experiments.context: In this experiment, you estimate how many beans are in a jar by marking some, mixing them back and scooping again. Scientists use the same trick to count fish and tigers.
experiments.question: If you mark 40 beans, mix them back into a jar and scoop again, can the number of marked beans in the scoop tell you how many beans are in the whole jar?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess how many beans are in the jar just by looking. Then guess whether a few scoops can give a better answer than your eyes. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every scoop uses the same small spoon, and you shake the jar the same way before each scoop. You return all the beans to the jar each time, so the jar never changes. Only the scoop changes, so any difference between estimates comes from chance, and from how many scoops you take.
results_table: Estimate of the jar: M times C divided by R

materials.item: a clean jar or steel dabba that holds about 1 litre, with a lid

about 240 dried white chickpeas (kabuli chana), which show a marker dot clearly. Dark rajma hides the dot, so use it only with a white marker or correction pen, counted out by a grown-up before the experiment
a washable marker pen, to make a dot on each bean
a small steel serving spoon or a small cup that holds about 30 to 45 chickpeas when heaped (test it first. A katori is too big for 240 beans, and an ordinary tablespoon may hold only about 20)
a big plate or tray to tip the beans onto
a sheet of paper, a pencil, and a calculator if you have one
a folded slip of paper with the true number of beans, hidden under the jar lid

experiments.safety: Dried beans can choke a child under five, so keep them away from little ones. Do not eat the marked beans, and never eat raw rajma, which can make you ill. If anyone in the family is allergic to chickpeas or beans, let someone else handle them. Use the marker pen in an open room and keep the cap on when you are not using it.
experiments.record: Fill in the table with one row for each scoop. Write M, the number of beans you marked, at the top. At the end, write the average of your estimates, and the true number from under the lid.

setup.art: The dotted chickpeas being poured back into the jar, and the jar being shaken with the lid on.
setup.caption: 4. Pour them back. Shake the jar well.

setup.art: A second scoop of chickpeas on a plate, with a few dotted ones pushed to one side, and a child writing numbers in a table.
setup.caption: 5. Scoop again. Count all the beans and the dotted ones. Work out your estimate.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Beans in the Jar test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the jar of beans. Do not say how many there are. Ask for a guess, and a reason for it. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: This jar has beans in it, and I know how many. You do not. How many do you think there are? How did you decide?
flow.kid: Look at the jar. Guess how many beans. Why do you think so?

ask.q: How did you decide on your number?
good: I looked at how big the jar is.
I guessed how many would fit in my hand.
I compared it with a jar I know.

flow.parent: A grown-up counts the beans in tens the day before, puts exactly 240 in the jar, and writes the number on a folded slip hidden under the lid. Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. One child: the parent counts and hides the beans, the child does everything else. Two to four children: one scoops, one counts all the beans (C), one counts the dotted beans (R), one writes the table, and swap roles for each scoop. For a fair race, each pair can use its own jar and then compare averages.

flow.context: In this step, you take the first scoop and mark every bean in it.
flow.do: Scoop one spoonful of beans onto the plate. Count the beans in the scoop. Write the number as M. Put a dot on each bean with the marker.
flow.say: We take a scoop of beans and count them. Then we put a dot on each one. This is the number we marked.
flow.kid: Scoop some beans. Count them. This is M. Put a dot on each bean.
flow.parent: Test your spoon first by scooping from the jar and counting: it should hold about 30 to 45 chickpeas. If it holds fewer than 20 the dots are too few and the estimates swing wildly. If it holds more than 60, use a smaller spoon. M can be any number, as long as you count it exactly.

flow.context: In this step, you put the marked beans back and mix them well, because the trick only works if they are well mixed.
flow.do: Pour the marked beans back into the jar. Put the lid on. Shake the jar 20 times, turning it over and around. Wait a moment for the beans to settle.
flow.say: The marked beans must mix in with all the others. We shake the jar well. If they stayed at the top, the scoop would be unfair.
flow.kid: Pour the marked beans back. Put the lid on. Shake it 20 times.

check.q: Why must we shake the jar well before the second scoop?
options: So the marked beans mix evenly with the others
So the beans get a dot
check.why: If the marked beans stayed in one place, the second scoop would catch too many or too few of them, and the estimate would be wrong. A fair sample needs the marked beans spread through the whole jar.

flow.context: In this step, you take the second scoop, count the marked beans and work out your first estimate.
flow.do: Scoop one spoonful from the jar onto the plate. Count all the beans in it, and write the number as C. Count the dotted ones, and write the number as R. Work out M times C, then divide by R.
flow.say: Now the second scoop. How many beans in all? How many have a dot? If a fraction of this scoop is marked, a fraction of the whole jar is marked too.
flow.kid: Scoop again. Count all the beans. Count the dots. Work out the estimate.

check.q: You marked 40 beans. In the second scoop of 40 beans, 8 have a dot. About how many beans are in the jar?
check.why: 8 of the 40 beans in the scoop are marked, which is 1 in 5. The 40 marked beans are about 1 in 5 of the whole jar. So the jar holds about 5 times 40, which is 200. Picking 80 means adding instead of multiplying.

flow.parent: If R is 0, there is nothing to divide by. Put the beans back, shake, and scoop again. Write down that you had to do this, because it tells you something about small samples.

flow.context: In this step, you repeat the scoop several times and find the average, to see whether more samples give a better estimate.
flow.do: Put the scoop back, shake the jar, and scoop again. Do this 5 times in all. Fill in a row of the table each time. Then add up the estimates and divide by 5.
flow.say: One scoop can be lucky or unlucky. So we do five. Does every scoop give the same estimate? Why not?
flow.kid: Repeat the scoop five times. Write each estimate. Find the average.

ask.q: Why are your estimates not all the same?
good: Each scoop is a bit different by chance.
Sometimes more marked beans end up in the scoop.
The scoop is only a small part of the jar.

flow.parent: With 240 beans and a first scoop of about 40, single estimates typically fall between about 150 and 400. The average of five usually lands closer to the real number, though not always exact. A fairer method is to add up all five C values and all five R values, then work out M times total C divided by total R. Try both and see which is closer. If all five estimates are far from the truth, check that the jar was shaken well and the dots were not rubbed off. Averaging is how scientists make a sample more trustworthy.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Beans in the Jar test. You open the slip, compare it with your estimate, and say what you found.
flow.do: Open the slip under the lid and read the true number. Compare it with your average. Say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now the real number. How close was your guess from looking? How close was your average from the scoops? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Read the true number. Compare. Say what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: a few scoops tell you more than looking. What I saw: my average was close to the true number, but single scoops were far off. Why: each scoop shows the fraction of marked beans, and the fraction is about the same in the scoop as in the jar. Link to the card: Counting what you cannot see.

experiments.title: Second Life of Water: which used water can still grow a plant?
experiments.context: In this experiment, you water moong seeds with four kinds of water, including used water from the kitchen. You find out which used water can be given to plants and which cannot.
experiments.question: Which grows moong best: clean tap water, rice-washing water, water with a little washing-up liquid in it, or water with salt in it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess which cup will grow the tallest sprouts and which the shortest. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The seeds come from the same packet, the cups and paper towels are the same, and each cup gets the same amount of liquid at the same time of day. The cups sit side by side at one window. Only the liquid is different, so any difference comes from the liquid.
results_table: Height of the 3 tallest sprouts on day 6 (cm)
What the roots and leaves looked like

materials.item: 4 small katoris or plastic cups of the same size
8 sheets of kitchen paper towel, folded to fit the cups, or a layer of cotton wool
40 whole green moong seeds, from one packet
1 cup of cloudy water from the first rinse of rice
washing-up liquid, 1 teaspoon
table salt, 1 level teaspoon
tap water, 3 cups
a tablespoon, a teaspoon, a marker and sticky labels, and a ruler

experiments.safety: Do not taste any of the liquids. If anyone in the family is allergic to moong or other pulses, a grown-up handles the seeds. Pour the soapy and salty water down the drain at the end, not on garden plants. Wash your hands after touching the towels. A little white fuzz on the paper towel is mould, so do not breathe it in. A grown-up throws away the towels and seeds in a closed bag.

schedule.what: Guess. Make the four liquids and set up the four cups with 10 seeds each.
Add 1 tablespoon of each liquid to its cup. Look at the seeds.
Add 1 tablespoon of liquid. Count how many seeds have a root showing. Write it down.
Add 1 tablespoon of liquid to each cup.
Add 1 tablespoon of liquid to each cup.
Measure the 3 tallest sprouts in each cup. Draw one sprout from each. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. On day 6, draw one sprout from each cup, side by side, and colour the roots and leaves as they look.

setup.art: Four cups in a row labelled A, B, C and D, each with a folded paper towel and ten green moong seeds on top.
setup.caption: 1. Put a folded towel and 10 moong seeds in each of four cups.

setup.art: Four small glasses on a counter: clear tap water, cloudy rice water, water with a drop of soap, and water with salt, each labelled.
setup.caption: 2. Make four liquids: tap water, rice water, soapy water and salty water.

setup.art: A hand pouring 3 tablespoons of liquid into each cup with a tablespoon.
setup.caption: 3. Give each cup 3 tablespoons of its own liquid.

setup.art: The four cups side by side on a sunny windowsill, with a small calendar beside them.
setup.caption: 4. Put the cups side by side by a bright window. Add 1 tablespoon each day.

setup.art: A child measuring a green moong sprout against a ruler beside a cup.
setup.caption: 5. On day 6, measure the 3 tallest sprouts in each cup.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Second Life of Water test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the four liquids. Say what is in each one. Ask which cup will grow the tallest sprouts, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: These are four kinds of water. One is clean tap water. One is the water we rinsed rice in. One has a little washing-up liquid. One has a little salt. Which will grow the best moong? Why?
flow.kid: Four kinds of water. Which grows moong best? Which grows worst? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that water will be the best?
good: The rice water has food in it.
Clean water is the best for plants.
Salt is bad for plants, and so is soap.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. People often think rice water will win, and soapy water may surprise them.

flow.context: In this step, you make the four liquids. They must be the same strength each time, so the test is fair.
flow.do: Label four cups A, B, C and D. A is tap water. B is rice-washing water. For C, stir 1 teaspoon of washing-up liquid into 1 cup of tap water, gently, so it does not foam. For D, stir 1 level teaspoon of salt into 1 cup of tap water until it disappears.
flow.say: A is plain tap water. B is the cloudy water from rinsing rice. C has a teaspoon of washing-up liquid in a cup of water. D has a teaspoon of salt in a cup of water. Never taste any of them.
flow.kid: Make four liquids. Tap. Rice water. Soapy water. Salty water. Label them A to D.
flow.parent: Use the first, cloudiest rinse of the rice for B. Keep a glass of each liquid for the days ahead, covered, because you will need about 1 tablespoon of each for each of the next five days. Make a fresh batch on day 4 if the rice water smells sour. Use a separate spoon for each liquid, or rinse the spoon between them. One child: do all four cups. Two to four children: each child looks after one cup (water it, count, measure), and all four compare at the end. With four or more children, a pair can run a second set of cups so the results can be checked.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the four cups with seeds and give them their first drink.
flow.do: Line each cup with two folded paper towels. Spread 10 moong seeds on top, not touching. Pour 3 tablespoons of the right liquid into each cup. Put the cups side by side by a bright window.
flow.say: Everything is the same except the liquid. Same cups, same towels, same seeds, same window. Pour three tablespoons into each cup.
flow.kid: Put a towel in each cup. Spread 10 seeds. Add the right water.

check.q: Why do all four cups get the same number of seeds and the same amount of liquid?
options: So only the liquid is different
So all the cups look neat
So the seeds do not get lonely
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one cup had more seeds or more water, we would not know whether the liquid or the amount made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you water the cups each day and, on day 3, count how many seeds have sprouted.
flow.do: On days 2 to 5, add 1 tablespoon of the right liquid to each cup. On day 3, count the seeds that show a root in each cup. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Look at the cups each morning. Add one tablespoon of the right water. On day three, count how many seeds have a root. Is it the same in every cup?
flow.kid: Add one spoon to each cup every day. On day 3, count the sprouted seeds.
flow.wait: Add a spoon of liquid to each cup every morning, and look closely on day 3.
flow.parent: In hot weather the towels can dry out in a few hours. If the towel is dry to touch, add the same extra spoon to every cup in the evening, and write it down. In monsoon, if the towels turn slimy or fuzzy, change the towels in every cup the same way. A root is a thin white tip poking out of the seed. Moong usually sprouts in plain water within 2 days. If cup A has not sprouted by day 3, the seeds are old, and the test is not fair. Start again with fresher seeds.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Second Life of Water test. You measure the sprouts, compare the cups and say what you found.
flow.do: On day 6, measure the 3 tallest sprouts in each cup from the seed to the tip. Write them in the table. Draw one sprout from each cup. Say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.say: Measure the three tallest in each cup. Which cup did best? Which did worst? Was your guess right? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Measure the three tallest sprouts in each cup. Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: The sprouts in the salty-water cup were short and brown, and those in the tap-water cup were tall and green. What is the best explanation?
options: Salt in the water stopped the seeds growing well
Salt made the seeds too happy
Tap water has magic in it
check.why: Salt pulls water out of seeds and roots, so they struggle to drink. This is why salty groundwater, in places where sea water has seeped into the ground, harms crops. Picking the second option means thinking more of anything is always better.

flow.parent: On day 6, healthy moong sprouts on paper towel are typically about 3 to 8 centimetres tall. Typical results: tap water and rice water are both good, and rice water is often as good or a little better. Soapy water and salty water slow the sprouts, and may stop some seeds. If every cup looks the same, write that down. It may mean the teaspoon was too little to harm moong in 6 days, and you could try 2 teaspoons next time. Rice water is a good use for second-hand water. Soap and salt should not go on plants.

experiments.title: The Rain Pit Model: which layer lets rain soak in fastest?
experiments.context: In this experiment, you pour the same amount of water onto stones, sand, soil and pressed soil, and measure how much goes through. This shows what a recharge pit needs to be filled with.
experiments.question: When rain falls on the ground, which material lets it soak through fastest and most: stones, sand, loose soil or pressed-down soil?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess the order of the four, from the fastest to let the water through to the slowest. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each funnel is cut from the same kind of bottle, plugged with the same cloth and filled to the same height. You pour the same 100 millilitres in the same way and start timing at the same moment. Only the material is different, so any difference comes from the material.
results_table: Water still held in the material (millilitres)

materials.item: 4 plastic bottles of the same size, 500 millilitres or 1 litre
4 clear glasses or cups to catch the water
4 small pieces of thin cloth, about 10 centimetres square
2 cups of dry garden soil, from a flowerpot or the garden
2 cups of clean sand, from a hardware shop or a building site
2 cups of small stones, pebbles or aquarium gravel
a measuring cup or a small medicine measure that shows 100 millilitres (without one, 100 millilitres is about 7 level tablespoons, but a cup is easier for reading what is collected), and a spoon
a phone or a clock with a second hand, for timing
a pair of scissors for the grown-up, and a marker

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottles with scissors or a knife. Rub the cut edge with a spoon handle so it is not sharp. Do the experiment on a tray or in a sink, as it will drip. Wash your hands after touching the soil.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the four funnels in a row with a line showing the height of the material, and draw blue arrows to show how much water came out of each.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting a plastic bottle in half, with the top half turned upside down to make a funnel.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts four bottles. Each top half is a funnel.

setup.art: A small piece of cloth being pushed into the neck of an upside-down bottle half.
setup.caption: 2. Push a cloth plug into each neck so the material stays in.

setup.art: Four funnels standing in four glasses, filled with stones, sand, loose soil and pressed soil, each to the same marked line.
setup.caption: 3. Fill the funnels to the same line: stones, sand, loose soil and pressed soil.

setup.art: A hand pouring 100 millilitres of water from a measuring cup into one funnel, with a timer in the corner.
