setup.caption: 4. Pour 100 millilitres of water into one funnel and start the timer.

setup.art: Four glasses side by side with different amounts of water at the bottom, and a child measuring them.
setup.caption: 5. After 3 minutes, measure the water in each glass.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Rain Pit Model. You guess before you build the funnels.
flow.do: Show your child the four materials. Ask them to put the four in order, from the fastest to let water through to the slowest. Write the order down, and the reason for it.
flow.say: Here are stones, sand, loose soil and pressed-down soil. We will pour the same water on each. Which lets water through the fastest? Which the slowest? Why?
flow.kid: Stones, sand, soil, pressed soil. Which lets water through fastest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will be the fastest?
good: Stones have big gaps between them.
Sand is loose.
Soil is soft, so water will go through easily.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think soil will be fastest, because it is the 'real' ground.

flow.context: In this step, you build the four funnels. A grown-up cuts the bottles.
flow.do: A grown-up cuts each bottle across, about 12 centimetres below the cap. Turn each top half upside down. Push a small cloth plug into each neck. Stand each funnel in a glass.
flow.say: Each top half of a bottle is a funnel. The cloth plug lets water drip out but keeps the sand and soil in. Stand each funnel in its own glass.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts four bottles. Plug each neck with cloth. Stand them in glasses.
flow.parent: The cloth should sit snugly in the neck, but not be packed hard. If it is too tight, water will crawl through very slowly, and all four funnels will look alike. Use the same amount of cloth in each. A little fine sand may wash through the cloth the first time, so ignore it. If the cut-off funnel is shallow, the water may reach the rim above the pressed soil. If so, pour the 100 millilitres in 3 or 4 small pours in all four funnels the same way. One child: do the four funnels one at a time. Four children: each takes one funnel, and all pour on the word go while one grown-up calls the time. With two children, each does two.

flow.context: In this step, you fill the funnels with the four materials to the same height.
flow.do: Mark a line 6 centimetres above the cloth inside each funnel. Fill A with stones. Fill B with sand. Fill C with loose, dry soil. Fill D with the same soil, pressed down hard with a spoon, then topped up to the line.
flow.say: All four are filled to the same line. A is stones. B is sand. C is loose soil. D is the same soil as C, but pressed down hard, like a path walked on every day.
flow.kid: Mark a line in each funnel. Fill with stones, sand, soil, and pressed soil.

check.q: Funnel C and funnel D hold the same soil to the same height. What is different about them?
options: D is pressed down, so it has less air space
D has a different kind of soil
check.why: Pressing squeezes out the air spaces between soil grains, and water travels through those spaces. Roads, roofs and trampled paths have the same effect, so rain runs off them instead of soaking in.

flow.context: In this step, you pour the same rain into each funnel and time what happens.
flow.do: Start with funnel A. Pour in 100 millilitres of water in about 5 seconds. Start the timer. Write the time of the first drip. After 3 minutes, measure the water in the glass. Do the same for B, C and D, one at a time, and write the numbers.
flow.say: Pour in the water evenly and start the timer. When does the first drip fall? After three minutes, how much water is in the glass? Is the rest still in the funnel?
flow.kid: Pour in 100 millilitres. Start the timer. Watch for the first drip. Measure the water at 3 minutes.
flow.parent: Pour as steadily as you can, and measure the water collected by pouring it from the glass into the measuring cup. Water still held is 100 minus what you collected. Very dry soil can soak up water at first, so these numbers are about, not exact. Typical: the stones let almost all the water through in a few seconds. Sand lets most through within a minute. Loose soil is slow, and pressed soil is slower, with a puddle on top. Exact numbers will differ. If no water comes through D at all, write 0 and note the puddle. That is a result too.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rain Pit Model. You compare the four funnels and say what you found.
flow.do: Put the funnels in order, from the most water to the least. Check your guess from step 1. Say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Which funnel let the most water through? Which the least? How did your order compare? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Put the funnels in order. Was your guess right? Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: A recharge pit under a terrace downpipe is filled with stones and sand, not soil. Why?
options: Stones and sand let rain pass through to the ground below
check.why: Stones and sand have big gaps for water to travel through, so rain passes down quickly instead of lying on the top. Soil holds water and passes it on slowly, and pressed soil hardly passes it at all.

flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: stones let the most water through and pressed soil the least. What I saw: nearly all the water ran through the stones in seconds and almost none ran through the pressed soil. Why: the gaps between the grains are big in stones and small in pressed soil. Link to the card: Groundwater is a bank account.

activities.title: Ask an Elder: what was here when you were my age?
activities.context: In this activity, you interview an older person about what their neighbourhood was like when they were a child. You then compare their answers with yours and find out how memory can hide a slow change.

materials.item: a grandparent, an older neighbour or an older shopkeeper who has lived near you for many years
paper, a pencil and a ruler, to draw a then-and-now table
old photographs of your street or town, if the family has any (optional)
a phone, to record the answers if the elder agrees (optional)

schedule.what: Write five questions. Ask an elder the questions. Write down their answers.
Fill in the then-and-now table. Talk about what could be checked.

activities.record: A then-and-now table with a row for each question: birds seen, where water came from, trees and green space, fish or insects. Add one line at the bottom for each thing you could check with a record.

setup.art: A child with a notebook sitting beside a grandmother on a verandah, with a cup of tea between them.
setup.caption: 1. Write five questions. Sit with an elder.

setup.art: A page divided into two columns, then and now, with rows for birds, water, trees and fish, and a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a then-and-now table.

setup.art: A child holding an old photograph of a street up beside the same street today.
setup.caption: 3. If you have an old photo, hold it next to the same place now.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ask an Elder. You prepare your questions and make your own guess first.
flow.do: Write five questions on a sheet of paper. Ask about birds, water, trees, and fish or insects they saw as a child. Add one question: how did you know?
flow.say: We will ask someone older what this place was like when they were small. First, what do you think it was like? Write your own guess.
flow.kid: Write five questions. Ask about birds, water, trees and fish. Guess the answers.

ask.q: Which of your five questions do you think will have the most different answer?
good: The one about birds.
The one about water.
The one about trees.

flow.parent: Choose a person who has lived near you for thirty years or more. Keep the questions simple and open. Do not suggest answers. A phone recording is useful, but ask permission first. One child: the parent writes while the child asks. Two to four children: share the five questions between them, or each child interviews a different elder and you compare tables.

flow.context: In this step, you interview the elder and write down their answers, including how sure they are.
flow.do: Ask your five questions, one at a time. Write down each answer in their words. Ask: how many, and how do you know? Write down if they say they are not sure.
flow.say: Please tell us what this place was like when you were my age. How many birds? Where did you get water? Which trees were here? How do you remember?
flow.kid: Ask each question. Write down the answer. Ask, how do you know?
flow.think: How is the answer different from what you see today?
flow.parent: Let the elder talk. Do not correct them, or say what you see today. Write down places, names and numbers, and also write down when they say they are not sure. If they mention a pond, a well or a tree, ask whether it is still there.

flow.context: In this step, you fill in the then-and-now table, with your own answers beside the elder's.
flow.do: Fill in the left column with the elder's answers. Fill in the right column with what you see today. Look at the rows where the two columns differ most.
flow.say: Let's put what we heard on the left and what we see now on the right. Where is the biggest difference? Which row surprises you?
flow.kid: Fill in your table. Elder on the left. Today on the right. Where is the biggest difference?

ask.q: Which row shows the biggest change?
good: The birds.
The water.
The number of trees.

flow.context: This is the last step of Ask an Elder. You think about how to check what an elder remembers and how this connects to the shifting baseline.
flow.do: Ask the questions below. Then write down one thing you could check with a record, such as an old photo, a map or a bird count.
flow.say: People who grow up with fewer birds think that is normal. How could we find out if the elder is right? What record could we look at?
flow.kid: How could you check what the elder said? What record could you look at?

check.q: A child grows up seeing few sparrows and thinks that is how it has always been. Her grandmother remembers many. What is this called?
check.why: A baseline is the amount we start from. Each generation takes the nature they first met as normal. So a slow loss is not noticed. Records, like old photos or bird counts, help us to check.

flow.think: What would you want a child 50 years from now to remember about today?

activities.title: Borewell in a Tub: how pumping lowers the water for everyone nearby
activities.context: In this activity, you make a model of the ground with sand and water, and take water out of one well. You watch what happens to the water in a second well nearby.

materials.item: a clear plastic box, tub or large jar with straight sides, holding about 1 litre or more
3 to 4 cups of clean sand (more for a wide tub, so it should make a layer about 6 centimetres deep)
1 litre of water in a jug, and a teaspoon
a marker pen and a ruler
2 drops of blue food colour (optional)
a tray to stand the tub on
2 short tubes of stiff card (a rolled and taped strip of card about 3 centimetres across and 8 centimetres tall), with a few holes poked near the bottom, to keep the wells open

schedule.what: Build the tub, fill it with water, pump out one well and watch the other. Pour in rain and watch it refill.

activities.record: A drawing of the tub from the side at the start, after pumping and after rain. Mark the water level on each. Write the heights in centimetres.

setup.art: A clear tub filled with sand, with two holes dug against the front wall, one at each end.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the tub with sand. Dig two holes against the clear wall.

setup.art: A jug pouring water slowly into the sand until the water shows in both holes, with a marker line on the outside of the tub.
setup.caption: 2. Pour water until both holes show water. Mark the level on the wall.

setup.art: A spoon taking water from the left hole, and the left hole nearly empty while the right hole is lower than before.
setup.caption: 3. Spoon water out of the left hole. Watch the right hole.

setup.art: A child dripping water from a spoon onto the sand in the middle, with the levels rising slowly again.
setup.caption: 4. Pour rain slowly onto the sand. Watch the levels rise.

flow.context: This is the first step of Borewell in a Tub. You build the tub and guess what will happen before you pump.
flow.do: Fill the clear tub with about 6 centimetres of damp sand. Stand a card tube in each end against the front wall, and pack damp sand around and between them. (Plain holes in sand tend to collapse, so the tubes keep the wells open.) Ask your child to guess what will happen to the other hole when you empty one.
flow.say: The sand is the ground. Each hole is a well. If we take water out of the left well, what will happen to the right well? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill the tub with sand. Dig two holes by the wall. Guess what will happen.

ask.q: If we pump water from one well, will the other well change? Why?
good: Yes, because the water is connected under the sand.
No, because the wells are far apart.
I'm not sure.

flow.parent: Damp sand stays in place better than dry sand. If you skip the tubes and dig plain holes, they may collapse, which the tubes avoid. Measure the water depth in each well by dipping a ruler or pencil to the bottom and reading the wet mark. One child: do all the jobs. Two to four children: one pumps, one measures each well, one writes, and swap after each round.

flow.context: In this step, you fill the ground with water, up to a level you can mark.
flow.do: Pour water slowly onto the sand until the water in both holes is 3 centimetres above the bottom. Draw a line on the outside wall of the tub at the level of the water. Write the height of each hole.
flow.say: We are adding rain to the ground, until the water table is 3 centimetres high. Mark it. This is our starting point.
flow.kid: Pour water slowly. Stop when both holes show 3 centimetres of water. Mark the line.
flow.parent: If the sand sucks up all the water, keep pouring slowly. It can take a cupful. Stop when you can see water standing in both holes.

flow.context: In this step, you take water out of the left hole and watch what happens in the right hole.
flow.do: Use the teaspoon to scoop water out of the left well. Do 10 scoops, quickly. After each 3 scoops, measure the water level in both holes. Write the heights down.
flow.say: Now we are the borewell. Take out water from the left hole, fast. What is happening in the left hole? What is happening in the right hole?
flow.kid: Spoon water from the left hole. Do 10 scoops. Measure both holes.

check.q: You spooned water from the left hole, and the water in the right hole also fell. What does this show?
options: The wells share one water table under the ground
check.why: The water in the sand is joined, so taking it from one place lowers it nearby. This is why a new borewell can dry up an old well next to it.

flow.parent: Typical: the left well empties and the right well falls, often by half or more, though it varies with the sand. Wet sand drains slowly, so wait a minute and measure again. If the right hole barely moves, the sand may be very coarse or wet. Move the holes closer together and try again.

flow.context: In this step, you add rain to the ground and see how slowly the water comes back.
flow.do: Drip 5 spoons of water slowly onto the sand in the middle, about one spoon every 10 seconds. Measure both holes at the end. Write the heights down.
flow.say: Now the monsoon comes. Rain soaks in slowly. Does the water come back as fast as we pumped it out?
flow.kid: Drip rain on the sand. Five spoons. Measure both holes.
flow.parent: The water comes back slowly, and not as fast as it was taken out. This is the point of the model. Pumping can be fast. Recharge is slow.

flow.context: This is the last step of Borewell in a Tub. You draw the three stages and think about where the water table goes.
flow.do: Draw the tub from the side three times: at the start, after pumping, and after the rain. Mark the water level in each drawing. Ask the question below.
flow.say: What happens to a city that pumps water fast and lets only a little rain soak in? What could it do?
flow.kid: Draw the tub three times. Start, pumping, rain. Mark the water.
flow.think: Near the sea, what do you think might creep into the ground if the fresh water falls too low?

activities.title: Seed Packets: save seeds from the kitchen
activities.context: In this activity, you collect seeds from vegetables and fruit that your family eats, dry them and keep them in labelled packets. This is what a seed bank does.

materials.item: seeds from two or three of: a tomato, a pumpkin, a papaya, a chilli, a lemon, a cucumber, a bitter gourd
a small sieve or tea strainer, and a bowl of water
newspaper or paper towels to dry the seeds on
small paper envelopes, or squares of paper folded into packets
a pencil to write the name and date on each packet
a dry tin with a lid to keep the packets in

schedule.what: Collect the seeds. Rinse them. Spread them on paper in the shade to dry.
Check that the seeds are dry. Pack and label them. Store them in the tin.

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the vegetables and fruit. Chilli seeds sting the eyes and skin, so wear gloves or wash your hands very well with soap, and keep them away from your eyes. Keep small seeds away from children under five.
activities.record: A list of the packets: name of the plant, where the seeds came from, date, and number of seeds. Add a note on what you would do with the seeds.

setup.art: A cut tomato and a spoon scooping seeds into a small sieve over a bowl, with the seeds and pulp.
setup.caption: 1. Scoop the seeds into a sieve. Rinse off the pulp.

setup.art: Seeds spread in a single layer on a piece of newspaper by a window, out of direct sun.
setup.caption: 2. Spread the seeds on paper in the shade. Leave them for 3 days.

setup.art: A small paper packet with a name and a date written on it, and a tin with a few packets inside.
setup.caption: 3. Fold a packet. Write the name and date. Store it in a tin.

flow.context: This is the first step of Seed Packets. You collect seeds and rinse them.
flow.do: A grown-up cuts open the vegetables or fruit. Scoop the seeds into the sieve. Rinse under running water, rubbing off the pulp. Wash your hands afterwards.
flow.say: Every seed is a plant waiting to grow. Let's save some from what we are eating. Rinse the pulp off, because it can make them rot.
flow.kid: Scoop out the seeds. Rinse off the pulp. Wash your hands.
flow.parent: Chilli seeds sting. Wear gloves or wash your hands very well with soap, and keep them away from eyes. Use seeds from a variety you like. Many shop tomatoes and chillies are hybrids, so their seeds may grow into plants that differ from the fruit. Local or traditional kinds usually grow the same as their parents. Tomato and papaya seeds are slimy, so rub them in a sieve under running water, and dry them on a plate, not paper, or they stick. Count the seeds each fruit gave and compare. One child: choose two fruits. Two to four children: each child takes a different fruit.

flow.context: In this step, you spread the seeds out to dry. Dry seeds keep much longer than damp ones.
flow.do: Spread the seeds in a single layer on paper. Put them in the shade, where air can reach them, and not in direct sun. Stir them once a day for 3 days.
flow.say: Seeds that stay damp go mouldy. They need to dry, in the shade, for a few days. Why do you think we keep them out of strong sun?
flow.kid: Spread the seeds on paper. Put them in the shade. Stir them each day.
flow.wait: Leave the seeds to dry for 3 days. In damp monsoon weather you should dry them indoors near a fan and give them 5 to 7 days. Put a spoon of dry rice in the tin to soak up moisture.

ask.q: Why do you think damp seeds are a problem?
good: They can go mouldy.
They can start to grow too early.
They can rot.

flow.context: In this step, you pack the dry seeds into labelled packets and store them.
flow.do: Check that the seeds are dry and hard. Fold each kind into its own packet. Write the name, the date and where they came from. Store the packets in the tin, in a cool, dry place.
flow.say: Now we are a seed bank. Each packet has a name and a date. Why does the date matter?
flow.kid: Fold a packet for each kind. Write the name and date. Put them in the tin.

check.q: Why do seed banks store seeds dry and cool?
options: Dry, cool seeds stay alive for longer
Dry seeds are lighter to carry
check.why: Seeds are alive but resting. Damp and warm seeds use up their stored food, or rot, and die sooner. Dry, cool seeds rest for years. That is why large seed banks use cold rooms.

flow.think: If you planted your packet next year, would every seed grow? How could you test that?

activities.title: Fingerprints and Stripes: how scientists tell one tiger from another
activities.context: In this activity, you make fingerprint cards of yourself and your family, mix them up and match them. This shows how scientists use stripe patterns to tell tigers apart in camera trap photos.

materials.item: a soft pencil (2B or darker) and white paper
clear sticky tape
3 or more family members who agree to give a fingerprint (if there are only 2 people, use two different fingers each, for example thumb and index finger, to make 4 sets)
a magnifying glass (optional)
a photo of a tiger's side or a drawing of stripes, if you can print one (optional)

schedule.what: Make fingerprint cards for three people. Mix them up. Match them. Talk about tigers.

activities.record: A card for each person, with their fingerprint taped on. A note of how you matched them.

setup.art: A pencil rubbed onto a patch of paper to make a dark grey square, and a child pressing a finger on it.
setup.caption: 1. Rub a pencil patch. Press a finger onto it.

setup.art: A piece of clear tape pressed onto the finger and then stuck onto white paper, showing a clear fingerprint.
setup.caption: 2. Lift the print with tape. Stick the tape on white paper.

setup.art: Six fingerprint cards spread on a table, with a child pointing at two that match.
setup.caption: 3. Mix up the cards and find the matching pairs.

flow.context: This is the first step of Fingerprints and Stripes. You make the fingerprint cards.
flow.do: Rub the pencil on paper to make a dark patch. Press one finger onto the patch. Press clear tape onto the finger, then lift it and stick it on white paper. Write the person's name on the back. Make two prints for each person.
flow.say: Everyone's fingerprint is different. We will make two prints of each person, and then try to match them. Press gently.
flow.kid: Rub a pencil patch. Press your finger. Lift the print with tape. Do it twice.
flow.parent: Use the same finger for both prints. Make the prints with the same pressure. A magnifying glass shows the ridges well.

flow.context: In this step, you mix up the prints and try to match each one to its twin.
flow.do: Turn the cards face down and mix them. Turn them up. Match each print to its twin. Check by turning them over to see the names. Count the right matches.
flow.say: Look closely at the lines. Where do they split, loop or swirl? Match each print with its twin. How many can you get right?
flow.kid: Match the prints. Look at loops and swirls. Check the names.

check.q: Why can scientists tell one tiger from another by their stripes?
options: Each tiger has a different stripe pattern
All tigers have the same stripes
check.why: Like fingerprints, the pattern of stripes is different on every tiger, and the pattern does not change over her life. So a photo from a camera trap is like a fingerprint card.

flow.parent: Write down how many you matched out of the total. Smudged prints are hard to match, which is a good thing to talk about: camera trap photos can be blurry too. Two to four children: each makes a set, and the others try to match them.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fingerprints and Stripes. You connect the fingerprints to counting tigers.
flow.do: Ask the questions below. If you have a tiger photo, compare the stripes on two photos.
flow.say: Scientists put cameras in a forest. Each photo shows a tiger's stripes. How can they tell how many different tigers there are, without ever touching one?
flow.kid: How can stripes show how many tigers live in a forest?

ask.q: How can photos show how many different tigers there are?
good: Each tiger has different stripes, so you can count the different patterns.
If the same stripes appear again, it is the same tiger.
You count the patterns that are not the same.

flow.think: If a tiger walked past the camera twice, how would you know it was the same one?

activities.title: Flower Watch: who visits the flowers?
activities.context: In this activity, you watch one flowering plant for 10 minutes at three times of the day and count which visitors come. If you have no flowering plant, this is for a day when you can find one nearby.

materials.item: a flowering plant on a balcony, in a school, or beside a road, such as hibiscus, tulsi, jasmine or marigold
a clock or phone timer
a sheet of paper and a pencil, ruled into columns for bee, butterfly, ant, fly, bird and other

schedule.what: Watch for 10 minutes in the morning. Make a tally. Choose your flower.
Watch for 10 minutes at midday. Make a tally.
Watch for 10 minutes in the evening. Compare the three tallies.

activities.record: A tally table with morning, midday and evening, and the number of each kind of visitor. A note of which time was busiest.
activities.safety: Stay a step back from bees and wasps and do not swat them. Do not touch a nest. If anyone in the family is allergic to bee stings, watch from indoors through a window.

setup.art: A child sitting a step back from a hibiscus bush on a balcony, with a clock and a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Sit a step back from a flowering plant with a clock and a tally sheet.

setup.art: A tally table with three rows labelled morning, midday and evening and columns for each visitor.
setup.caption: 2. Make a tally table with a column for each kind of visitor.

setup.art: A bee, a butterfly and a sunbird visiting a flower while a child makes tally marks.
setup.caption: 3. For 10 minutes, make a mark for each visit.

flow.context: This is the first step of Flower Watch. You choose a plant, make a guess and do your first count.
flow.do: Choose one flowering plant. Ask your child to guess who will visit, and when. Sit a step back. Watch for 10 minutes, and make a tally mark for each visit.
flow.say: We will watch one plant. Who do you think will visit it? When will she get most visitors, morning, midday or evening? Why?
flow.kid: Pick a flower. Guess who comes and when. Watch for 10 minutes.

ask.q: When do you think the plant will have the most visitors, and why?
good: In the morning, because bees wake early.
At midday, because it is warm.
In the evening, because it is cooler.

flow.parent: Count a visit each time a creature lands on a flower. Do not count one that only passes. Do not worry if few come. Write down zero if no one comes. If few or no visitors come, try another plant (marigold, tulsi in flower, ixora or a flowering weed often draw more), and also count the open flowers so that counts can be compared. Write the weather and whether the flower was in sun or shade. One child: watch and tally alone. Two to four children: one watches the clock, one tallies, and each takes a different plant or time.

flow.context: In this step, you do the midday count in the same way.
flow.do: Sit in the same place at midday. Watch the same plant for 10 minutes. Make a tally mark for each visit.
flow.say: Same plant, same place, different time. Who is here now? Is it busier or quieter?
flow.kid: Watch the same flower at midday. Tally the visitors.
flow.parent: Use the same plant and the same spot, so the counts can be compared.

flow.context: This is the last step of Flower Watch. You do the evening count and compare the three.
flow.do: Watch for 10 minutes in the evening. Add up each column. Find the busiest time. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which time was the busiest? Who visited most? What do the visitors take from the flower, and what might they give back?
flow.kid: Watch in the evening. Add up. Which time was busiest?

check.q: A bee visits a flower for nectar and carries pollen to the next flower. What does this help the plant do?
check.why: Pollen carried from one flower to another lets the flower make seeds and fruit. When flowers lose their visitors, many crops make less fruit.

flow.think: What would happen to a plant that lost all her visitors?

projects.title: Kitchen Seed Bank: which seeds in my kitchen are still alive?
projects.context: In this project, you test six kinds of seeds from the kitchen to see how many sprout. You find out which are alive and which are not, which is the test a real seed bank does.

materials.item: 10 whole green moong seeds
10 pieces of split moong dal
10 whole kala chana (black chickpeas), raw
10 roasted chana, the ready-to-eat kind
10 mustard seeds and 10 fenugreek (methi) seeds
6 small plates or katoris, and paper towels
a marker and 6 labels, a spoon and some water

projects.safety: Keep the seeds away from children under five, as they can choke on them. Do not eat the sprouted seeds from a damp towel. If anyone in the family is allergic to pulses, mustard or fenugreek, a grown-up handles those seeds. Do not sniff mouldy towels. Throw them away in a closed bag. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Guess. Count 10 of each seed onto a damp paper towel in its own plate.
Look. Add a spoon of water if the towel is drying. Count the sprouted seeds.
Look. Add water if needed. Count the sprouted seeds.
Look. Add water if needed. Count the sprouted seeds.
Count the sprouted seeds. Work out the percentage for each. Draw a bar chart. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

projects.record: A table with a row for each seed and a column for each day you counted. At the end, work out the percentage of seeds that sprouted: sprouted seeds, divided by 10, times 100. Draw a bar chart.

setup.art: Six plates each with a folded damp paper towel, and ten seeds of a different kind on each, with labels.
setup.caption: 1. Put 10 seeds of one kind on a damp towel in each plate. Label the plates.

setup.art: The six plates side by side on a shelf, with a calendar showing days 1 to 8.
setup.caption: 2. Keep the plates side by side. Add a spoon of water if the towel dries.

setup.art: A child counting the seeds with white roots in each plate and writing numbers in a table.
setup.caption: 3. Count the sprouted seeds every day or two.

setup.art: A bar chart of six bars with different heights, one for each seed.
setup.caption: 4. On day 8, work out the percentage and draw a bar chart.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Seed Bank. You guess which seeds are alive before you test them.
flow.do: Lay out the six kinds of seeds. Ask your child to guess how many of 10 will sprout from each kind, and why. Write the guesses in a table.
flow.say: Here are six kinds of seeds from our kitchen. Some are alive, and some are not. How many of ten do you think will sprout from each? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the six seeds. Guess how many of ten will sprout. Why?

ask.q: Which seeds do you think will not sprout, and why?
good: The roasted chana, because it has been cooked.
The split dal, because it is broken.
The old seeds, because they are dried out.

flow.parent: Do not say which seeds are alive. Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the six plates, with ten seeds of one kind in each.
flow.do: Fold a paper towel in each plate and wet it until it is damp but not dripping. Count 10 seeds of one kind onto each. Label each plate with the name of the seed. Put the plates side by side.
flow.say: Each plate gets one kind of seed, and ten seeds. We keep the towel damp, and the plates side by side. Then only the seed is different.
flow.kid: Put a damp towel in each plate. Count 10 seeds. Write the name on the plate.

check.q: Why do all six plates get 10 seeds, the same kind of towel and the same water?
options: So only the kind of seed is different
So the seeds are not lonely
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the plates had different towels or water, we would not know whether the seed or the plate made the difference.

flow.parent: Mustard and methi seeds are tiny. Count them onto the tip of a spoon. The towel should be damp like a wrung-out cloth, not wet. Too much water rots seeds. One child: set up all six plates. Two to four children: each takes 1 or 2 plates, and everyone checks all the plates together on the counting days. Old seeds from the back of the kitchen may sprout less well than fresh ones, and that is a real result. In hot weather check the towels twice a day.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the plates over several days, and count the seeds with a white root showing.
flow.do: On days 2, 3 and 5, look at each plate. Add a spoon of water if the towel is dry. Count the seeds that have a white root. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Look at each plate. A sprouted seed has a small white root poking out. Count them. Are all the plates the same?
flow.kid: Look at each plate. Count the seeds with white roots. Write the numbers.
flow.wait: Look at the plates on days 2, 3 and 5.
flow.parent: Moong and mustard usually sprout within 2 days, and chana in 2 to 3. The split dal and roasted chana will not sprout, and may go mouldy or smell sour. Throw those away in a closed bag when you are done.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Kitchen Seed Bank. You work out the percentage for each kind and say what you found.
flow.do: On day 8, count the sprouted seeds in each plate. For each, divide the number by 10 and multiply by 100 to get the percentage. Draw a bar chart. Say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.say: For each plate, how many of ten sprouted? That is the percentage. Which seeds are alive? Which are not? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count the sprouts. Work out the percentage. Draw a bar chart.

ask.q: Why did some seeds not sprout?
good: The roasted chana was cooked, so it died.
The split dal was broken, so the baby plant inside was damaged.
Those seeds were old.

flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: whole raw seeds are alive, and roasted or split ones are not. What I saw: most of the whole moong, kala chana, mustard and methi sprouted, and none of the roasted chana or split dal. Why: a seed holds a tiny plant, and heat or breaking kills it. Seed banks test their seeds in the same way every few years.

challenges.title: Rain Home: send the roof's rain into the ground
challenges.problem: Build a model house from a box, with a roof, a gutter and a pipe. Pour 500 millilitres of rain over the roof. Send as much of it as you can into a recharge pit, so that very little runs away across the table.
constraints: Use only things from home, with no tape on the pit, and nothing bought for this.
Pour the rain from a mug over the roof in 20 seconds, the same way each time.
The pit must be a cup or tub filled with stones and sand, standing in a tray of soil.
Measure the water that runs away into a tray. The less it is, the better.
materials: a shoebox or small carton, and thin cardboard for the roof
an old plastic bottle cut in half lengthways, or folded foil, for the gutter
a straw or a rolled paper tube for the downpipe
a cup, small tub or half-bottle for the pit, with stones and sand
a tray, a mug of water and a measuring cup
general: A sloping roof with a gutter along the lower edge, and a pipe from the gutter into the pit.
A pit with stones at the bottom and sand on top, as in the Rain Pit Model.
A lip or tray around the pit to catch drops that bounce.
creative: Two roofs sloping towards the same gutter, to catch more rain.
A small filter of cloth at the top of the pit, to stop leaves and dirt from blocking the stones.
A second pit for any overflow, joined to the first by a channel in the soil.
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle and the cardboard. Rub the cut edges with a spoon handle so they are not sharp. Do the pouring over a tray or a sink.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and pour on 500 millilitres of rain. Measure the water that ran away. Change one thing, such as the gutter or the slope, and test again. Which design sent the most water to the pit? Why do you think so?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about rainwater harvesting. You build a model house and try to send its rain into the ground.

setup.art: A child sketching a house with a sloping roof, a gutter, a downpipe and a pit under the ground.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch your house, gutter, pipe and pit.

setup.art: A shoebox house with a cardboard roof, a half-bottle gutter and a straw pipe leading to a cup of stones in a tray of soil.
setup.caption: 2. Build the house, gutter, pipe and pit in a tray.

setup.art: A mug pouring water over the roof while another tray catches the water that runs away.
setup.caption: 3. Pour 500 millilitres over the roof. Measure what runs away.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Rain Home challenge. You read the problem and plan two designs.
flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two designs, and to guess how much water each will send to the pit.
flow.say: Your house has a roof, a gutter and a pit. Rain must go from the roof to the pit with as little as possible running away. Sketch two ideas.
flow.kid: Read the problem. Sketch two designs. Guess how much water reaches the pit.

ask.q: What could make the rain run past the pit?
good: A gutter with a gap.
A pit that is too small.
A roof that is too steep, so the water shoots over the gutter.

flow.context: In this step, you build your first design and test it with 500 millilitres of rain.
flow.do: Build your first design in the tray. Pour 500 millilitres from a mug over the roof in 20 seconds. Measure the water that ran away. Subtract it from 500 to find the water that reached the pit.
flow.say: Pour the rain over the roof. How much ran away across the tray? How much reached the pit? Write it down, so you have something to beat.
flow.kid: Build your house. Pour the rain. Measure what ran away.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the bottle and the cardboard. Some water will stay on the roof and in the cup. That is fine. The first number is the one to beat.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rain Home challenge. You change one thing, test again and think about real homes.
flow.do: Change one thing in your design. Pour 500 millilitres again. Measure again. Compare the two numbers. Ask the question below.
flow.say: What did you change? Did more water reach the pit? In a real city, what would stop rain from reaching the ground?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Which design was better?

check.q: In a real city, why does less rain soak into the ground than in a forest?
options: Roofs and roads send the rain into drains
Rain falls more slowly in cities
City soil is made of stone
check.why: Roofs, roads and pavements are hard, so rain runs off them into drains and out to sea. A forest floor soaks the rain in. A recharge pit gives the rain a way back to the ground.

challenges.title: Write the Fishing Rule: a rule a whole village will follow
challenges.problem: Three villagers share one pond for 8 years. Write a rule that all three will follow, so that the pond stays alive and the village catches at least 40 fish in all. Test your rule with the Pond Council game.
constraints: The rule must fit on two lines of paper and be easy to follow.
The rule must say how many fish each villager can catch.
The rule must say what to do in a bad year.
Test the rule over 8 years. The pond must stay alive and the village must catch at least 40 fish.
materials: the Pond Council board and the fish tokens
two or three people, one for each villager
general: A fixed limit, such as every villager may catch 2 fish a year.
A rest year, where nobody fishes in a year when the pond has fewer than 12 fish.
A rule to always leave 16 fish in the pond, and to share the rest.
creative: A limit that depends on the pond, such as: catch half of the fish above 16, and share them equally.
A watcher who counts the fish each year and tells the village the limit.
A fair rule for the last year, so nobody is tempted to take everything.
challenges.your_turn: Write your rule. Play the game with it for 8 years. Did the pond stay alive? How many fish did the village catch? Change one thing in the rule and try again. Which rule worked best, and why?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about rules for shared things. You write a rule for a village pond and test it in the Pond Council game.

setup.art: A child writing a two-line rule on paper beside a pond board with fish tokens.
setup.caption: 1. Write your rule in two lines.

setup.art: Three players taking fish from the pond according to the rule, with the year marker on the board.
setup.caption: 2. Play 8 years, with everyone following the rule.

setup.art: A table of catches and pond counts, with a tick for a pond still alive.
setup.caption: 3. Count the fish. Did the pond stay alive?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Fishing Rule challenge. You write your first rule.
flow.do: Read the problem. Write a rule in two lines. Guess how many fish the village will catch in 8 years with your rule.
flow.say: You are the village council. You must write one rule that everyone follows. What will it say? How many fish will the village catch?
flow.kid: Write a two-line rule. Guess how many fish you will catch.

ask.q: Why might a rule that says take 2 fish each be a problem?
good: It might be too many if the pond is low.
It does not change in a bad year.
It is the same for a big pond and a small pond.

flow.context: In this step, you play 8 years of Pond Council following your rule, and count the result.
flow.do: Reset the pond to 16 fish. Play 8 years. Every villager follows the rule. Count the fish in the bowls at the end, and write down if the pond stayed alive.
flow.say: Everyone follows the rule, with no cheating. Play it through. Is the pond alive at the end? How many fish did you catch?
flow.kid: Reset the pond. Play 8 years with your rule. Count the fish.
flow.parent: A rule of 2 each collapses the pond in about 5 years. A rule to always leave 16 fish gives about 56 fish. A rule of 1 each is safe but only gives 24.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Fishing Rule challenge. You change the rule and think about who might break it.
flow.do: Change one thing in your rule. Play again, or work it out on paper. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: What if one villager breaks the rule in Year 5? How would the village find out? What should happen to them?
flow.kid: Change your rule. Try again. What if someone cheats?

check.q: A rule that nobody watches is broken by one villager. Why does this matter for the whole village?
options: The pond can be emptied by one person's extra catch
The pond grows faster when someone cheats
check.why: In a shared pond, the cost of one person's extra catch falls on everyone. That is why successful commons have ways of watching and agreeing on fair penalties, as Elinor Ostrom found.

flow.think: Who should watch the pond, and how should the village decide?

items.p: Which of these can be used for ever, if we take no more than nature replaces each year?
opts: Fish in a lake
Coal under the ground
Iron ore in a mountain
items.why: Fish have young every year, so a lake can keep giving fish if enough are left to breed. Coal and iron ore took millions of years to form. Picking them means thinking everything natural grows back.

items.p: A pond gains 8 new fish every year, and the villagers catch 8 fish every year. What happens to the number of fish over the years?
opts: It stays about the same
It keeps growing
It keeps falling
items.why: What comes in equals what goes out, so the stock stays steady. If the catch were bigger than the new fish, the pond would slowly empty.

items.p: The number of fish in a pond right now is called the ____ of fish.
items.why: A stock is how much of something there is right now. The births and the catch are flows that change the stock.

items.p: Priya says, 'Fish can have young, so a lake of fish can never run out.' Is she right?
items.why: False. Fish can run out if the catch is bigger than the births, or if too few parents are left. Renewable only works if we take less than nature replaces.

items.p: Meena marks 20 beans and mixes them into a jar. She scoops 30 beans and finds 5 marked ones. About how many beans are in the jar?
opts: About 60
About 120
About 150
items.why: 5 of the 30 beans in the scoop are marked, which is 1 in 6. The 20 marked beans are about 1 in 6 of the jar. So the jar holds about 6 times 20, which is 120. Picking 150 means adding when you should multiply.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Renewable resource
nature makes it again within a lifetime
Non-renewable resource
takes millions of years to form
Stock
how many there are right now
Sample
a small part used to learn about the whole
Habitat
where a living being finds food, water and shelter
items.why: These words are the tools for talking about taking from nature. A strong answer could add an example for each word.

items.p: Sort each of these. Is it renewable, or not renewable?
items.why: Things that living beings or the weather make again within years are renewable. Fuels and ores took millions of years, so for people they are not renewable.

items.p: Put the steps of mark and recapture in order.
items: Scoop again and count the marked beans
Put a dot on every bean in the first scoop
Mix the dotted beans back into the jar
Scoop some beans and count them
a: Scoop some beans and count them
Put a dot on every bean in the first scoop
Mix the dotted beans back into the jar
Scoop again and count the marked beans
items.why: You must count and mark the first group, mix it back in well, and only then take the second sample to see what fraction is marked.

items.p: A scientist marks 100 fish in a lake and lets them go. Later she catches 50 fish, and 10 of them are marked. About how many fish are in the lake?
opts: About 250
About 500
About 1,000
items.why: 10 of the 50 fish are marked, which is 1 in 5. The 100 marked fish are 1 in 5 of the lake, so the lake holds about 5 times 100, which is 500.

items.p: A group of animals falls to very few, and people stop hunting them. Why might they still not recover?
opts: Too few parents are left to have enough young
The animals forget how to breed
The forest will not let them back
items.why: Young come from parents. With very few parents, few young are born, and the few animals may be too far apart to find each other. Picking 'forget' puts a human habit on an animal.

items.p: A forest cut in two by a road is the same for the animals as one big forest of the same total size.
items.why: False. Each half is smaller, each group of animals is smaller, and crossing the road is dangerous. A corridor or an underpass can join the halves again.

items.p: Which of these is a protected place that a village, not the government, has kept for hundreds of years?
opts: A sacred grove
A zoo
A tiger reserve gate
items.why: Villages in Kerala, Karnataka, Meghalaya and other states kept sacred groves for hundreds of years. Zoos and tiger reserves are run by the government.

items.p: A place that keeps seeds dry and cold, so a crop can be grown again if it is lost, is called a seed ____.
items.why: A seed bank keeps copies of seeds safe, like a bank account for crops. India's national gene bank is in New Delhi.

items.p: A fisher has a full basket of clams every day, but the clams in it are smaller each year. Explain what this might mean for the lake.
items.a: The basket may be full of more, smaller clams. Small clams have not yet grown big enough to have young. So there may be fewer parents left in the lake, and the lake may be being overfished.
items.why: A strong answer says that the size, not only the number, tells us about the lake, and that small clams have not had time to breed.

items.p: Draw a bath with a tap and a drain. Label the tap 'births' and the drain 'catch'. Show the water as the number of fish in a pond.
items.art: A blank bath with a tap and a drain.
items.a: A bath with water in it, a tap labelled births running water in, and a drain labelled catch letting water out. The water level is labelled the fish in the pond.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the water stays level only when the tap and the drain run at the same speed.

items.p: Two children in Kochi are talking about the sea, where their uncles fish.

views.says: The sea is so big that nobody could empty it. The boats can catch as much as they like.
Even a big sea can run low if the boats catch more than the fish can replace. We need a rule.

items.ask: Which child do you agree with? Use what you know about stocks and parents. Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer says that Farhan is right that fish can run low when the catch is bigger than the births, and that the sea is large but not endless. Lakshmi is right that the sea is big, and that it has many fish.
items.why: Both children have part of it. A strong answer uses the idea of stock and births, not only the size of the sea.

items.p: Which of these is an example of the shifting baseline?
opts: A child who has never seen a big flock of sparrows thinks a few sparrows is normal
A scientist counting beans in a jar
A farmer drying seeds in the shade
items.why: A baseline is what we start from. Each generation takes the nature they first met as normal, so slow loss goes unnoticed. The other two are a way of counting and a way of saving seed.

items.p: In a district, rain soaks in and adds 60 units of water to the ground each year, and the wells take out 80 units. What happens to the water table over the years?
opts: It falls
It rises
It stays the same
items.why: More goes out than goes in, 80 against 60, so the stock falls by 20 units every year. Like a bank account, a balance falls if you take out more than you put in.

items.p: Why can digging a deeper borewell fail to solve a water shortage in the long run?
opts: It takes more from the same shrinking store of water
Deeper water is always dirty
Deeper wells make less rain
items.why: A deeper well reaches lower water, but if the store keeps falling, the new well also runs dry in time. Recharge is what fills the store again.

items.p: When too much fresh water is pumped from the ground near the sea, sea water can slowly seep into the ground and make wells salty.
items.why: True. Fresh water pushes back the salt water. When the fresh water level falls, the salt water can move in. This has been reported near some coastal cities.

items.p: Sort each action. Does it help groundwater recharge, or does it lower the water table?
items: a pit of stones under a terrace downpipe
many new borewells dug close together
paving over an open courtyard completely
a small earth dam holding monsoon rain on the land
cleaning and refilling the temple tank
draining all the rain from the roads into the sea
items.why: Anything that lets rain soak in refills the store. Anything that pumps faster or sends rain away before it soaks in lowers it.

items.p: Match each protected idea to what it is.
pairs: Sacred grove
a patch of forest kept by a village for hundreds of years
Oran
a village pasture kept for grazing and trees in Rajasthan
Tiger reserve
a large area where tigers and their prey are guarded by law
Wildlife corridor
a strip of habitat that joins two forests
Seed bank
a store that keeps seeds dry and cold
items.why: Protection can be made by law or by a community. A strong answer could say which of these is a place, which is a path, and which is a store.

items.p: Which method can count how many tigers live in a forest, without disturbing any of them?
opts: Camera traps, with each tiger recognised by her stripes
Asking one villager for a guess
Counting one footprint on a path
items.why: Every tiger has a different stripe pattern, so photos from many cameras show how many different tigers there are. One guess or one footprint is too little.

items.p: The habit of taking the amount of nature we grew up with as normal is called the shifting ____.
items.why: The word was used by a fisheries scientist in 1995. A baseline is the starting point we measure from, and it shifts with each generation.

items.p: In a game, a pond holds at most 24 fish. 20 fish are left after the catch. For every 2 fish left, 1 new fish is born. How many fish are in the pond after breeding?
opts: 24 fish
30 fish
20 fish
items.why: 20 fish make 10 pairs, so 10 new fish would be born. 20 plus 10 is 30, but the pond holds only 24. The pond is full, and the extra fish have no room.

items.p: A village grows five kinds of rice. A disease strikes one kind. A neighbouring village grows only that kind. Which village is safer, and why?
opts: The five-kind village, because four kinds survive
The one-kind village, because its farmers know that rice well
Both are safe, because the disease will go away
items.why: A disease usually harms one variety more than others. With five kinds, most of the harvest survives. With one kind, the whole harvest can fail.

items.p: Put these in the order they happen when too many fish are caught year after year.
items: Fewer young fish are born each year
The catch is bigger than the births
The pond holds very few fish
a: The catch is bigger than the births
Fewer young fish are born each year
The pond holds very few fish
items.why: Each step causes the next. Taking too many leaves fewer parents, fewer parents have fewer young, and the stock falls further.

items.p: A bigger catch in the boats always means there are more fish in the lake.
items.why: False. A bigger catch can come from more boats, finer nets or going further. A scientist looks at the catch for each hour of fishing, and at the size of the fish.

items.p: Garrett Hardin said that shared things are used up. Elinor Ostrom found many villages that looked after theirs for hundreds of years. In your own words, what do the villages that succeed seem to do?
items.a: They set rules together, they know who may use the shared thing, they watch each other and they punish cheating fairly. They talk often, and the people who use the commons help to make the rules.
items.why: A strong answer names at least two things villages do, such as making rules together and watching for cheating, and does not say that shared things always fail.

items.p: Explain why a recharge pit under a downpipe is filled with stones and sand, and not with soil.
items.a: Stones and sand have big gaps between them, so rain passes through quickly and soaks down to the ground. Soil holds water and passes it on slowly, and pressed soil hardly passes any.
items.why: A strong answer connects the size of the gaps to how fast water moves, as in the funnel test.

items.p: Draw the tub model of groundwater at three stages: at the start, after pumping out one well, and after the rain. Mark the water level in each.
items.art: Three blank rectangles side by side, each with sand drawn at the bottom and two holes against the wall.
items.a: At the start both holes have water at 3 centimetres. After pumping, the left hole is almost empty and the right hole is lower. After the rain, both holes are slightly higher but not as high as the start.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that both holes fall when one is pumped, and that rain refills them more slowly than pumping emptied them.

items.p: Two children are talking about a plan to bring cheetahs from Africa to a national park in India.

views.says: Bring them back. India lost its cheetahs, and the grasslands need big hunters.
Spend the money on animals that still live here, like the great Indian bustard.

items.ask: Which child do you agree with? What evidence would you want before you decide? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side but names evidence such as how many cheetahs survive, how the grasslands change and what the money would otherwise do. It gives credit to the other side.
items.why: This is a debated question. A strong answer uses evidence and fairness, and does not claim that one side is simply foolish.

items.p: Ravi marks 30 fish, and later he catches 60 fish. Of these, 4 are marked. About how many fish are in the lake?
opts: About 120
About 450
About 1,800
items.why: 4 of the 60 fish are marked, which is 1 in 15. The 30 marked fish are about 1 in 15 of the lake, so the lake holds about 15 times 30, which is 450.

items.p: In a mark and recapture count, some of the marked fish die before the second catch. How does this change the estimate?
opts: The estimate comes out too high
The estimate comes out too low
The estimate does not change
items.why: Fewer marked fish are left to be caught, so the second catch has fewer marks than it should. A smaller fraction marked makes the lake seem bigger than it is.

items.p: In a mark and recapture count, the marked fish are brighter and easier to catch than the others. How does this change the estimate?
opts: The estimate comes out too low
The estimate comes out too high
The estimate does not change
items.why: More marked fish are caught than a fair sample would give, so the fraction marked looks bigger. A bigger fraction marked makes the lake seem smaller than it is.

items.p: A pond holds fish, and the rule is that 1 new fish is born for every 2 left after the catch. 16 fish are in the pond, and three villagers catch 4 fish each. After breeding, ____ fish are in the pond.
items.why: The three villagers catch 12 fish, which leaves 4. 4 fish make 2 pairs, so 2 new fish are born. 4 plus 2 is 6. The pond has almost emptied in one year.

items.p: A group that falls to very low numbers can take much longer to recover than one that falls only a little, even when both are fully protected.
items.why: True. With very few parents, few young are born, and the survivors may be far apart or related. The cod of Newfoundland took a very long time to recover after the fishery was stopped in 1992.

items.p: In a pond that holds at most 24 fish, with 1 new fish for every 2 left, the biggest steady catch comes from leaving ____ fish after each catch.
items.why: 16 fish make 8 pairs, so 8 new fish are born, and the pond is full again at 24. The village can then take 8 fish every year for ever.

items.p: A lake may be fished too hard. Sort each of these. Is it a sign of overfishing, or not a sign?
items: the fish in the market get smaller every year
boats must go further out to fill their baskets
the monsoon came a week early
a new fish market opened in town
it takes longer to catch the same number of fish
the price of rice went up
items.why: Signs of overfishing show that the fish are fewer or smaller: smaller fish, more effort for the same catch and longer trips. The weather and the prices of other things do not tell us about the fish.

items.p: Which is the best reason to keep an old variety of rice that few farmers grow today?
opts: It may carry a trait, such as standing floods, that a new rice needs
It always gives more grain than new rice
It is easier to sell than new rice
items.why: Old varieties hold useful traits that breeders can use. A flood-tolerant rice from Odisha was used to breed a modern rice. The other reasons are not always true.

items.p: Three of these are careful ways to find out how many there are of something. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Camera trap photos matched by stripes
Counting beans in samples from a jar
Marking and releasing tagged fish
Asking one person how many they think there are
items.why: The first three use a method that can be repeated and checked. One person's guess depends on memory and may be influenced by the shifting baseline.

items.p: Rain falls 20 millimetres deep on a terrace of 30 square metres. 1 millimetre on 1 square metre is 1 litre. So ____ litres of rain land on the terrace.
items.why: 20 millimetres on 1 square metre is 20 litres. On 30 square metres it is 30 times 20, which is 600 litres.

items.p: A borewell's water level falls 3 metres every year. A recharge pit adds back 1 metre every year. After 5 years the level has fallen a total of ____ metres.
items.why: Each year the net fall is 3 take away 1, which is 2 metres. Over 5 years, 5 times 2 is 10 metres. Recharge slows the fall, but does not stop it.

items.p: The boundary of a tiger reserve drawn on a map is the edge of where a tiger can live.
items.why: False. Tigers walk across the boundary, so they need the forest outside as well as inside. This is why corridors and the land around a reserve matter.

items.p: A fisher says, 'My basket is full every day, so the lake is fine.' Write what you would measure to check, and why.
items.a: I would measure the size of the fish, how long it takes to fill the basket and how far the boats must go. If the fish are smaller, or the trips are longer, the lake may be overfished even if the basket is full.
items.why: A strong answer names at least two measures that do not depend on the basket, and says why.

items.p: Describe one way a mark and recapture estimate could go wrong, and how you would make your estimate better.
items.a: The marked beans might not mix well, so the second scoop has too many or too few. I would shake the jar well, take a bigger scoop and repeat the scoop many times and take the average.
items.why: A strong answer names a real problem, such as poor mixing or marked animals dying, and a fix such as more samples or a better mix.

items.p: Draw a line graph over 20 years of the size of the biggest fish caught each year. Draw one line for a lake that is overfished, and another for a lake that is well looked after.
items.art: A blank graph with years along the bottom and fish size up the side.
items.a: The overfished line slopes steadily downwards over the 20 years. The well-looked-after line stays roughly level, with small ups and downs.
items.why: A strong graph shows that the size of the biggest fish falls in an overfished lake because fish are caught before they can grow, and stays steady in a well-managed one.

items.p: Two children are talking about a village pond that every family uses for fishing.

views.says: If a pond is shared, everyone will take too much. We need a guard and a fine for those who cheat.
The families who use the pond know each other. If they make the rules together, they can keep it healthy.

items.ask: Which child do you agree with? What would you want to know about the village before you decide? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer says that both ideas appear in real life. Guards and fines help when people do not know each other, and shared rules help when a community is small and trusts each other. It names what it would want to know, such as how many families there are.
items.why: This is a debated question. A strong answer uses the Hardin and Ostrom ideas and does not say that one child is simply wrong.

quiz.p: A pond makes 6 new fish a year, and the village catches 9 fish a year. What will happen to the pond over time?
opts: The number of fish will fall
The number of fish will stay the same
The number of fish will rise
quiz.why: More fish leave the pond than are born, so the stock falls each year. When there are fewer parents, fewer young are born, and the fall can speed up.

quiz.p: What does a scientist do in mark and recapture?
opts: Marks some animals, lets them go, catches a second sample, and uses the fraction marked to estimate the whole group
Counts every animal one by one
Weighs all the animals in the group
quiz.why: Mark and recapture works when counting every animal is impossible. The fraction of marked animals in the second sample is about the same as the fraction marked in the whole group.

quiz.p: A jar holds 50 marked beans among all its beans. A scoop of 20 beans has 5 marked ones. About how many beans are in the jar?
opts: About 100
About 200
About 500
quiz.why: 5 of the 20 beans in the scoop are marked, which is 1 in 4. The 50 marked beans are 1 in 4 of the jar. So the jar holds about 4 times 50, which is 200.

quiz.p: Which of these can be used for ever, if we take no more than nature replaces?
opts: Trees in a managed forest
Coal
Petrol
quiz.why: Trees grow back within years, so a forest can last if we cut no more than grows. Coal and petrol took millions of years to form.

quiz.p: A small group of tigers lives in a forest cut into separate patches. Why is this dangerous for the tigers?
opts: Few parents can find each other, so few young are born
The tigers forget how to hunt
The patches get too much sunshine
quiz.why: Small, cut-off groups have few parents, and the tigers may be too closely related. A corridor that joins the patches lets them meet and move.

quiz.p: Which of these is a village rule that protects nature?
opts: No fishing for one month while the clams release their young
Taking as much as you can before others do
Cutting the biggest tree in the grove
quiz.why: A closed season gives the animals time to have young. Taking as much as possible, or cutting the biggest tree, takes away the parents.

opts: The top of the water stored in the ground
A table for water jugs
The pipe that carries water to a house
quiz.why: Water soaks into the tiny spaces in sand and rock, and the top of that water is the water table. It rises with recharge and falls when we pump more than refills.

quiz.p: A disease kills one kind of rice in a village that grows five kinds. What is most likely to happen?
opts: The other four kinds keep growing, so most of the harvest survives
All the rice dies
The disease helps the other rice grow
quiz.why: A disease usually harms one variety more than others. This is why farmers who grow many varieties are safer. Seed saved from the lost kind could grow that rice again.

quiz.p: A fisher brings home the same weight of fish every day, but the fish are smaller each year. What does this suggest?
opts: The fish are being caught before they grow and have young
The fish are getting healthier
The lake is getting bigger
quiz.why: Smaller fish mean younger fish. If fish are caught young, fewer reach the age to breed. The weight in the basket can hide this.

opts: Each generation takes the nature they grew up with as normal, so slow loss goes unnoticed
A line that moves when you measure it
A way to count fish by marking them
quiz.why: A baseline is the amount we start from. If it shifts with every generation, we may not notice a loss that happened over many years. Records and old photographs help.

quiz.p: Elinor Ostrom studied many real commons. What did she find?
opts: Many communities managed shared things well for hundreds of years by making their own rules
Shared things are always used up
Only governments can manage shared things
quiz.why: Ostrom found that communities with clear rules, ways of watching and fair penalties could look after commons. She won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2009 for this work.

quiz.p: Why do scientists who count animals usually give a range, such as between 400 and 600, and not one exact number?
opts: A sample is always a little different from the truth
They are not sure how to count
They want to make the number look big
quiz.why: Each sample gives a slightly different estimate. A range shows how much the estimate could vary, and a bigger sample gives a narrower range.

Water boards measure wells every year to see if the water table is rising or falling.
City planners add recharge pits, lakes and open ground, so rain can refill groundwater.
Seed banks keep copies of crop varieties, and plant breeders use old varieties to make crops that stand floods, drought or disease.

Pollster teams ask a sample of people to guess how a whole town or country will vote.
Museums and libraries keep old records, photographs and specimens, so that later scientists can compare the past with the present.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living beings are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: About two million kinds have been named, but most small beings such as insects, fungi and bacteria have never been counted. Estimates range from several million to many millions.

open_questions.q: How low can a group of animals fall before it cannot recover?
open_questions.why_open: Some groups recover from a few animals and others do not. Scientists are still working out why, and it seems to depend on the kind of animal, her food and her habitat.

open_questions.q: Is there one right number of tigers for a forest?
open_questions.why_open: The number depends on the amount of prey, the size of the forest and the people living around it. Scientists, villagers and governments weigh these differently, and there is no single agreed answer.

open_questions.q: Can a lost kind of animal be brought back, and should we try?
open_questions.why_open: Reintroducing animals has worked in some places and failed in others. Bringing back a kind that is extinct is still only an idea, and people argue about whether it is wise.

open_questions.q: How can we know the true size of a stock we can never see all at once?
open_questions.why_open: Every method has some error. Scientists keep improving counting methods and checking them against each other, and they disagree about how far to trust an estimate.

open_questions.q: How much water is stored deep under India, and how fast does it refill?
open_questions.why_open: Deep groundwater is hard to measure, and some of it fell as rain thousands of years ago. Measurements of deep aquifers are still uncertain in many regions.

open_questions.q: Why do some shared things last for hundreds of years, while others are used up?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found rules that often help, but they have not found a recipe that works everywhere. Each community and each resource is a little different.

jokes.j: Why did the stones win the rain race?

jokes.j: Why did the grandmother count the fish by the size of the biggest one?

maths.problem: Chitra marks 36 beans and mixes them into a jar. She scoops 45 beans and finds 9 marked. About how many beans are in the jar?
maths.explain: 9 of the 45 beans are marked, which is 1 in 5. The 36 marked beans are about 1 in 5 of the jar. So the jar holds about 5 times 36, which is 180.
maths.context: This is about the Beans in the Jar test, where you mark some beans and scoop again.
maths.why_maths: The fraction of marked beans in the scoop tells us the fraction of the jar that is marked, so we can scale up to the whole jar.

maths.problem: Five scoops from a jar gave these estimates of the number of beans: 200, 320, 240, 180 and 260. What is the average? Which single estimate was farthest from the average?
maths.answer: The average is 240. The estimate of 320 was farthest, 80 away.
maths.explain: 200 plus 320 plus 240 plus 180 plus 260 is 1,200. 1,200 divided by 5 is 240. 320 is 80 more than 240, and 180 is 60 less, so 320 is farthest.
maths.context: This is about the Beans in the Jar test, where you repeat the scoop five times and find the average.
maths.why_maths: An average of many estimates is usually closer to the truth than one estimate, because lucky and unlucky scoops cancel out.

maths.problem: A pond holds 24 fish. For every 2 fish left after the catch, 1 new fish is born, and the pond holds at most 24. The village catches 10 fish. How many are in the pond next spring? What if the village catches 8 fish?
maths.answer: With a catch of 10, there are 21 fish. With a catch of 8, there are 24 fish.
maths.explain: After 10 are caught, 14 are left. 14 fish make 7 pairs, so 7 are born, and 14 plus 7 is 21. After 8 are caught, 16 are left. 16 make 8 pairs, so 8 are born, and 16 plus 8 is 24, which is full.
maths.context: This is about the Pond Council game, where a village shares a pond and the fish breed each year.
maths.why_maths: Working out the next year shows that a catch of 8 keeps the pond full while a catch of 10 leaves it smaller, so a small difference adds up.

maths.problem: A terrace is 8 metres long and 6 metres wide. 25 millimetres of rain falls on it. A tank holds 1,000 litres. How many litres of rain land on the terrace, and how many tanks would it fill?
maths.answer: 1,200 litres, which is 1 full tank and a fifth of a second tank.
maths.explain: The area is 8 times 6, which is 48 square metres. 1 millimetre on 1 square metre is 1 litre, so 25 millimetres on 48 square metres is 48 times 25, which is 1,200 litres. 1,000 litres fills one tank, and 200 litres is one fifth of another.
maths.context: This is about the Rain Pit Model and the Rain Home challenge, where rain from a roof is sent into the ground.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the area of a roof by the depth of rain tells us how much water we could save, so we can size a tank or a pit.

maths.problem: A district has 300 units of water stored underground. Each year, rain adds 55 units and wells take out 80 units. How many units does the store lose each year, and how many years until it is empty?
maths.answer: It loses 25 units each year, and it is empty in 12 years.
maths.explain: 80 take away 55 is 25, so the store falls by 25 each year. 300 divided by 25 is 12, so it is empty after 12 years.
maths.context: This is about the Borewell in a Tub activity, where pumping is faster than the rain that refills the ground.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting what goes in from what goes out gives the yearly loss, and dividing the store by the loss predicts when it runs out.

maths.problem: In the Kitchen Seed Bank, 9 of 10 moong seeds sprouted, 7 of 10 methi sprouted, and 0 of 10 roasted chana sprouted. What is the percentage for each? Which would you keep in a seed bank?
maths.answer: Moong 90 percent, methi 70 percent and roasted chana 0 percent. I would keep the moong, and I would not keep the roasted chana.
maths.explain: A percentage means out of 100. 9 out of 10 is 90 out of 100. 7 out of 10 is 70 out of 100. 0 out of 10 is 0. Seeds that sprout are alive, so the moong is best to keep. Roasted chana was cooked, so it cannot grow.
maths.context: This is about the Kitchen Seed Bank project, where you test how many seeds of each kind are alive.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets us compare seed tests, even when different numbers of seeds were tested, and tells a seed bank when to renew a stock.

maths.problem: The biggest fish landed in a market was 60 centimetres long in the first year of records, and 36 centimetres long 30 years later. By what fraction of its length did the biggest fish shrink?
maths.explain: 60 take away 36 is 24. 24 out of 60 is 24 over 60, which simplifies to 2 over 5. The biggest fish shrank by two fifths of the first length.
maths.context: This is about the shifting baseline, where slow changes in the size of fish are hard to notice without records.
maths.why_maths: A fraction turns a change in size into one number that can be compared between different lakes and different years.

maths.problem: Suppose a reserve had about 1,400 tigers in one count, and about 3,000 in a count 16 years later. About how many times as many is that? About how many more tigers were there for each year, on average?
maths.answer: About 2 times as many, and about 100 more each year.
maths.explain: 3,000 divided by 1,400 is a little more than 2, so about 2 times. 3,000 take away 1,400 is 1,600. 1,600 divided by 16 is 100, so about 100 more each year.
maths.context: This is about the way scientists compare counts of animals from different years, using rounded numbers.
maths.why_maths: Rounding both counts makes it easy to see the size of the change in your head, and dividing by the years shows how fast it happened.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet run at home with children. Beans in the Jar: the numbers were worked out by simulating many scoops. With 240 beans and a first scoop of about 40, single estimates often fall between 150 and 400, and the average of five is usually within 15 percent of the true number. The parent must count the beans in tens the day before, and should not let the child see the number. Second Life of Water: soap and salt at 1 teaspoon in a cup of water usually slow or stop moong, and rice water is usually as good as tap water. If no cup shows a difference, say so, and try 2 teaspoons next time. Rain Pit Model: stones drain in seconds, sand in about a minute, loose soil slowly and pressed soil barely. Pond Council was checked by working out every year for three villagers. A greedy catch of 4 each empties the pond in two years. A catch of 2 each empties it in about five years. Leaving 16 fish gives a steady catch of 8 a year, and the best total over eight years is 64. Seed Keepers is a simple model and does not match real rice farming. Facts for a grown-up to verify before release: the tiger counts of about 1,400 in 2006 and more than 3,000 in 2022, the Ashtamudi clam fishery certification in 2014, the date of the cheetahs' arrival at Kuno, the flood-tolerant rice from Odisha, the Alwar johads, the number of national parks in India, and the ids for the three videos.
